case_summary: In N. Thamarai Bharathi @ Athisundarapandian vs Public Prosecutor, the petitioner faced defamation charges under Section 500 IPC. The allegations stemmed from a public speech in which the petitioner criticized the ruling party and made personal statements against the then Chief Minister. The complaint was filed under Section 199 Cr.P.C. by the Public Prosecutor. The petitioner contended that the statements were general political criticism without direct connection to the Chief Minister’s discharge of official duties, which should not attract defamation charges under Section 199(2) Cr.P.C.
case_decision: The Madras High Court quashed the defamation complaint, ruling that the statements did not have a reasonable nexus to the Chief Minister’s official duties and were more related to political criticism. Citing prior judgments, the court concluded that personal defamation claims should be pursued privately under Section 199(6) Cr.P.C. and not through a public prosecutor under Section 199(2). Therefore, the criminal proceedings against the petitioner were dismissed.

                                                       ORDER

This Criminal Original Petition has been filed to quash the private complaint filed against the petitioner for the offence under Section 500 I.P.C.

2. The crux of the allegation in the complaint indicates that the petitioner in a public speech has made certain defamatory statements against the then Chief Minister thereby caused damage to the reputation in the eye of the society. Hence, he sought to be prosecuted.

3. The transcribed version of the speech of the petitioner is spanning around ten pages. From a cursory perusal of the same, it is seen that statements have been made opposing the Ruling Party, except few sentences, which have also targeted the then Chief Minister in personal capacity has no nexus with the discharge of official duty. No statements have been made to attract the filing of the private complaint by exercising the power under Section 199 Cr.P.C. All the statements in his public meeting is targeted against the action of the Government.

2/8

https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Crl.O.P(MD)No.452 of 2020 Some statements have been personally made against the then Chief Minister. Therefore, the general statements questioning the action of the State cannot be construed as defamation of the individual. Further, the statements made in the individual capacity against the then Chief Minister have no nexus with the discharging of official duty. In this regard, this Court in M.K.Stalin vs. City Public Prosecutor (2020 0 Supreme(Mad) 1231), has held as follows:

“9. It is also to be noted that in a catena of judgments reported in[(2015)8 SCC 239 R A J D EE P S A R D E S A I VS. ST A T E OF AND H R A P R A D E S H AN D OTHER S] and[1993 Supp (1) SCC 499, the Apex Court held that judicial process should not be an instrument of oppression or needless harassment. In PEP S I FOODS LIM I TED VS. SPEC I A L JUDIC I A L M AG I S T R A T E REPO R TED IN (1998) 5 SCC 749, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that summoning of an accused in a criminal case is a serious matter and criminal law cannot be set into motion as a matter of course. The so called imputation allegedly made should have reasonable nexus with discharge of public duties. Therefore, mere criticism without any intent on the part of the petitioner and/or without any nexus with discharge of public duties will not come under the purview of offence punishable under Sec.500 3/8 https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Crl.O.P(MD)No.452 of 2020 of I.P.C.
....
11. In a judgment reported in (2018)6 SCC 676 [K.K.M I S H R A VS.THE ST A T E OF M A D HY A P A DE S H AND OTHER S the Apex Court held that the alleged statements have no reasonable nexus with the discharge of public duties by or office of the Chief Minister. Such statements may be defamatory but in absence of a nexus between the same and the discharge of public duties or office of the Chief Minister, remedy under section 199(2) and 199(4) Cr.P.C. will not be available. It is the remedy saved by the provisions of subsection (6) of section 199 Cr.P.C. i.e. a complaint by the Chief minister before the ordinary court i.e. the court of a Magistrate which would be available and could have been resorted to.

....

13. Similarly in KART A R S I NGH VS. ST A T E OF PUNJ A B reported IN A.I. R. 1956 SC 541 wherein the Apex Court held that vulgar abuses made against the Transport Minister and the Chief Minister will not amount to defamation of the State but may amount only to the defamation of the public functionaries concerned and therefore, they are only personal in nature. The facts of that case are that the accused was charged under section 9 of the 4/8 https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Crl.O.P(MD)No.452 of 2020 Punjab security of the State Act, 1953 for making vulgar abuses against the Transport Minister and the Chief Minister. The Hon’ble Supreme Court even though finding that the accused statements amounted to defamation against the Transport Minister and the Chief Minister however held that the vulgar abuses do not undermine the security of the state or friendly relations with foreign states nor did they amount to contempt of court or defamation prejudicial to overthrow the state. The Apex court held that the slogans were certainly defamatory of the Transport Minister and the Chief Minister, but the redress of that grievance was personal to these individuals and the state authorities could not take the cudgels on their behalf.

...

16. To take cognizance of the complaint under Section 199(2) of Cr.P.C., the so called defamation should be directly attributed to a person in discharge of his/her public functions and only in such circumstances, Sub Section 2 of Section 199 of Code of Criminal Procedure will stand attracted. If the said imputation apparently made against the pubic functionaries, in discharge of his/her public function, have no reasonable nexus with the discharge of public duties, the remedy available under Section 199(6) of Cr.P.C. before the Magistrate by making private complaint,and remedy under Section 199(2) and 5/8 https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Crl.O.P(MD)No.452 of 2020 199(4) will not be available. Otherwise, if any criticism or defamation in the nature of personal capacity and such defamation have no nexus with discharge of his/her official function of the State, complaint cannot be made by a Public Prosecutor merely on the basis of G.O.

4. Applying the above position of law, the entire general statements sought to be used as a defamation, do not fall within the ambit of defamation.

case_summary: in Sri Thimmappa Bhat vs. Shri T N Chikkarayappa, a private complaint was filed under Sections 500, 501, and 502 of the IPC, accusing the petitioner (Editor of the Vijayavani newspaper) of publishing defamatory statements. The complainant alleged that defamatory news, based on a report by accused No.1 (the reporter), was published in the daily newspaper. The petitioner argued that he resided outside the territorial jurisdiction of the Magistrate and that no preliminary inquiry, as required under Section 202(1) CrPC, was conducted. Furthermore, the petitioner asserted that the publication was made in good faith and without the intent to harm the complainant's reputation.
case_decision: The Karnataka High Court quashed the proceedings against the petitioner, ruling that there were no allegations of intent to harm or knowledge of harm to the complainant's reputation. Additionally, the Magistrate had failed to conduct a preliminary inquiry under Section 202(1) CrPC, as required when the accused resides outside the territorial jurisdiction. Thus, continuing the criminal proceedings would amount to an abuse of legal process. The petition was allowed, and the case against the petitioner was dismissed.

Author: Hemant Chandangoudar

Bench: Hemant Chandangoudar

BETWEEN:

       'VIJAYAVANI', VRL MEDIA LTD
       NO.124, 1ST AND 3RD FLOOR

(BY SRI ARUNA SHYAM M., SENIOR COUNSEL FOR

AND:

(R1 SERVED AND UNREPRESENTED)

     THIS WRIT PETITION IS FILED UNDER ARTICLES 226 AND
227 OF THE CONSTITUTION OF INDIA R/W SECTION 482 OF
CODE OF CRIMINAL PROCEDURE, PRAYING TO QUASH THE
                                  2



ENTIRE PROCEEDINGS INITIATED AGAINST THE PETITIONER IN
C.C.NO.22735/2018 ARISING OUT OF PCR NO.26358/2013 ON
THE FILE OF VIII ACMM - BENGALURU FOR THE ALLEGED
OFFENCES PUNISHABLE UNDER SECTIONS 500, 501 AND 502
OF IPC, 1860 AND ALL FURTHER PROCEEDINGS PURSUANT
THERETO, PRODUCED AT ANNEXURE-A AND B RESPECTIVELY
AND ETC.

     THIS WRIT PETITION COMING ON FOR PRELIMINARY
HEARING IN 'B' GROUP THIS DAY, THE COURT MADE THE
FOLLOWING:

                            ORDER

A private complaint was filed under Section 200 of Cr.PC for the offences punishable under Sections 500, 501 and 502 of IPC alleging that the petitioner, who is an Editor of Vijayavani, Kannada daily news paper, has published news item in the daily news paper against the respondent - complainant making defamatory statements and accused No.1 is the reporter of the said news item. The learned Magistrate after recording the sworn statement registered the case against the petitioner - accused No.2 and accused No.1 for the aforesaid offences. Taking exception to the same, the petitioner - accused No.2 is before this Court.

2. Sri Arun Shyam M, learned Senior counsel appearing for the learned petitioner's counsel submits that the petitioner - accused No.2 is residing outside the territorial jurisdiction of the 3 learned Magistrate and as such, the registration of the case without conducting a preliminary enquiry as specified under Section 202(1) of Cr.PC is impermissible. He further submits that the news item published in the daily news paper is out of good faith and not with an intention to harm or with knowledge or having reason to believe that it will harm the reputation of the person concerned. In support, he placed reliance on the decisions of the coordinate Bench of this Court in the case of the Editor, Deccan Herald -vs- Prof. M S Ramaraju reported in ILR 2005 Kar. 1907 and Mrs. Tara Ajai Singh -vs- Mr.R P Sharma reported in ILR 2012 Kar. 5619.

3. The respondent though served with notice has remained absent.

4. I have considered the submission of the learned counsel for the petitioner.

5. The allegations made in the private complaint filed by the respondent is that the petitioner - accused No.2 is an Editor of Vijayavani, Kannada daily newspaper and on the basis of the report of the accused No.1, who is the reporter of the said daily news paper, has published the derogatory news item against the 4 respondent. The coordinate Bench of this Court in the case of the Editor, Deccan Herald (supra) has held that in the absence of any allegation having been made in the news item against the respondent by the petitioner, it cannot be said that the publication of the said news item brings the case within the ambit of Section 499/401 of the IPC.

6. The coordinate Bench of this Court in the case of Mrs. Tara Ajai Singh (supra) has held that to constitute the offence of defamation, the imputation must have been made with an intention to harm or with knowledge or having reason to believe that it will harm the reputation of the person concerned. In the present case, there is no allegation that the petitioner - accused No.2 intentionally published the derogatory news item against the complainant with an intention to harm his reputation. Hence, in the absence of essential ingredient to constitute the commission of offence alleged against the petitioner - accused No.2, the registration of private complaint against the petitioner - accused No.2 is impermissible.

7. Even otherwise, the petitioner -accused was residing outside the territorial jurisdiction of the learned Magistrate and 5 the learned Magistrate was required to conduct preliminary enquiry before taking the cognizance as specified under Section 202(1) of Cr.PC. In the present case, the learned Magistrate without conducting a preliminary enquiry as specified under Section 202(1) of Cr.PC has taken cognizance of the offence alleged against the petitioner - accused No.2, and the same is contrary to Section 202(1) of Cr.PC.

In view of the preceding analysis, I am of the considered view that the continuation of criminal proceeding against the petitioner - accused No.2 will be an abuse of process of law. Accordingly, I pass the following:

ORDER
i) Writ petition is allowed;
ii) The impugned proceeding in CC No.22735/2018 pending on the file of the VIII ACMM, Bangalore City, insofar as it relates to petitioner - accused No.2 is hereby quashed.

Sd/-

case_summary: In L. Nandagopal Yadav vs. Mr. Udai Pratap Singh, the petitioner, Vice President of All India Yadav Maha Sabha (AIYMS), filed a defamation complaint under Section 500 IPC against the respondents, who were the President and Secretary of AIYMS. The petitioner alleged that a public notice published in the Tamil daily “Malai Malar” on 16.12.2016, announcing his suspension from AIYMS, defamed him. The petitioner claimed that the suspension was not communicated to him directly but through a public notice, causing embarrassment and harm to his reputation. He argued that the respondents violated the Sabha's bye-laws and sought damages for defamation.
case_decision: The Madras High Court dismissed the criminal revision petition, upholding the trial court’s decision to reject the defamation claim. The Court found that the respondents acted within their authority under the AIYMS bye-laws and that the public notice did not contain any defamatory imputation against the petitioner. It further held that the petitioner had not sufficiently demonstrated how the public notice harmed his reputation or met the legal requirements for defamation. The petitioner was advised to challenge the suspension through appropriate legal channels rather than filing a defamation case.

                       President, All India Yadav Maha Sabha
                       No.6, Mahatma Gandhi Road,

                     PRAYER: Criminal Revision Petition filed under Sections 397 and 401 of

                                                               ORDER

The petitioner filed a private complaint for the offence under Section 500 IPC against the respondents herein before the learned II Metropolitan Magistrate, Egmore, Chennai in C.M.P.No.718 of 2017. The Trial Court by order dated 23.05.2017 dismissed the complaint under Section 203 Cr.P.C. since no offence made out. Against which, the present revision petition is filed.

2.The respondents failed to appear before this Court, private notice sent was also returned with an endorsement ‘unclaimed’ and the name of the respondents printed in the cause list. Since the case is pending from the year 2017 for the service of notice and all the efforts went in vein, this Court appointed Mr.R.Ashwin Kumar, as Legal Aid Counsel for the respondents by order dated 11.04.2022.

2/12 https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Crl.R.C.No.834 of 2017

3.The gist of the complaint is that the complainant is a businessman, doing business of general commercial export business, he is also an income tax assessee for the past 36 years, he has got good reputation and he is also Vice President of All India Yadav Maha Sabha [AIYMS] having Headquarters at Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh. He was elected in the General Body meeting of the Association in the year 2007. As per the bye-law, the Annual General Body meeting to be convened once in a year, the respondents are the President and Secretary, who failed to convene the Annual General Body meeting and follow the bye law, hence the petitioner/complainant objected to the same. Offended over the same, the President and General Secretary of the AIYMS removed the petitioner from the post of Vice President of AIYMS. By removing the petitioner, they have violated the bye law. Further, the respondents caused an advertisement in the Tamil daily “Malai Malar” on 16.12.2016 informing the removal of the complainant from the post of Vice President which was read by general public and his business friends who enquired him about the same which caused embarrassment, disrepute for the petitioner. Thereafter, the petitioner issued a notice to the respondents on 17.12.2016 seeking the 3/12 https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Crl.R.C.No.834 of 2017 reason for giving such a public notice. Since no reply was received, the editor, reporter of Malai Malar were asked to produce the details of the person who has given the advertisement and the mode of payment which were also withheld. The publication in Malai Malar caused dis-reputation to the petitioner in the eyes of general public and his friends, thereby petitioner got defamed. The petitioner was concerned with the mismanagement of the funds of AIYMS for which he raised objection and without reasons, suspended from AIYMS. Since the public notice caused disrepute and defamed the petitioner, he filed a complaint of defamation. The petitioner examined himself as witness and produced documents. The petitioner further examined two witnesses, C.W.1 and C.W.2. The Trial Court finding no ground to presume that the accused have committed the offence, dismissed the complaint under Section 203 Cr.P.C.

4.The contention of the petitioner is that the order passed by the Trial court in dismissing the complaint is not justifiable either in law or on the facts of the case. The Trial Court ought to have taken cognizance of the offence on the complaint and issued summons to the accused. The Trial 4/12 https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Crl.R.C.No.834 of 2017 Court at the stage of entertaining the complaint is only to see whether prima facie case is made out and need not look into the materials to find out whether case would end in conviction. Further, the Trial Court given the reason that the public notice issued would fall under the 9th Exception to Section 499 IPC is not proper. This Court as well as the Apex Court have time and again held that when any defamatory material is sought to be defended under exemption, the same is a matter of fact, to be decided only in a trial. Further, it was stated that the petitioner acted against the interest of AIYMS and spreading false messages about AIYMS through various social media creating lot of confusion, disharmony and conflicts among the Sabha members are not supported with any materials. It is further submitted that making false allegation and advertising the same in the newspaper by public notice would amount to per se defamation. It is submitted that earlier to the public notice, the petitioner sent letters to the General Secretary of the Sabha from April 2015 and continuously following with the Secretary, President and others about the misappropriation/mismanagement of the Sabha funds by the office bearers in the guise of enrolling new members and District units. The respondents failed to take any effective action to rectify the 5/12 https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Crl.R.C.No.834 of 2017 defects, on the other hand expelled the petitioner. The respondents though received the notice, kept quiet and not replied to the same. Further, the petitioner relied upon the decision of the Kerala High Court in the case of M..N.Meera vs. A.C.Mathew and another reported in 2002 Cri.L.J. 3845, wherein it is clearly held that under 9th Exception to Section 499 IPC, the question whether the statement in question was made for public good is a matter to be considered based on prospective evidence, the burden lies on the accused and it is for him to adduce sufficient evidence which would enable an interference that there was some public good involved in the matter of particular statement.

5.The learned counsel for the respondents on the contrary submitted that the petitioner if aggrieved on his suspension from the post of Vice President of AIYMS, his grievance to be addressed by filing a civil suit questioning the same and not by filing a defamation case. It is submitted that the petitioner admits that respondents are the President and Secretary of AIYMS, as per the bye law they are empowered to take disciplinary action against the misconduct of its members and office bearers. The bye law is 6/12 https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Crl.R.C.No.834 of 2017 formulated in such a manner to effectively run the Sabha in a structured and orderly manner. It is further submitted that the Sabha consists of lakhs of members, if such control is not there, the functioning of the Sabha could not be in a orderly manner and total chaos would prevail. The petitioner had not questioned the authority of the respondents to take action for misconduct. The grievance of the petitioner is that the order of removal was not communicated to him and it was made by a public notice, which is not so. The order was sent to the petitioner by registered post. Further the Sabha consists of members in various walks of like, every nook and corner, sending communication to each and every member would take some time, to immediately inform the members about the functioning of the Sabha and the disciplinary action taken, public notice was issued. Since the office bearers of the Sabha take a public role among the members of the Sabha, it would be appropriate that such public notices are issued. Further, from going through the public notice nowhere any imputation was caused to the petitioner. It is only stated that since the petitioner acted against the interest of the Sabha and creating confusion among the members, he was kept under suspension for six years. In the meanwhile, he could very well challenge the 7/12 https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Crl.R.C.No.834 of 2017 same in the manner known to law and not by filing a defamation case.

6.It is further submitted that from the complaint as well as the sworn statement of the petitioner which was filed in the typed set of papers, it is seen that the petitioner had merely stated about the public notice dated 16.12.2016 and non-receipt of the suspension notice personally. case_summary: In Sri Mahendra Mishra vs. Sri Lalith Rao, the petitioner sought to quash criminal proceedings against him under Sections 384 (extortion) and 500 (defamation) of the IPC. The case arose from a news broadcast on TV 9, showing the respondent and his wife, which the respondent claimed was defamatory and part of an extortion attempt. The Magistrate took cognizance of the complaint and issued summons to the accused. While accused nos. 3 and 4 were later discharged due to insufficient evidence of extortion or defamation, the petitioner (accused no. 2) contended that the same reasoning should apply to him, arguing that the broadcast did not amount to defamation and that he was not responsible for the alleged extortion or the broadcast's content.
case_decision: The Karnataka High Court dismissed the petition, holding that the trial court should determine whether the broadcast constituted defamation and whether the petitioner was involved in extortion or the airing of the video.                         ORDER

Petitioner was a Director of a TV channel and a programme was aired on the said channel. Contending the same to be defamatory and also alleging that the petitioner and three others had tried to extort money, the complainant (respondent herein) filed a private complaint before JMFC (II Court), Mangaluru, Dakshina Kannada against the petitioner and three others for the offences punishable under Sections 384 and 500 of IPC. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offences and summons were issued to all the accused and CC No.1/2013 was registered. As the petitioner, who is accused no.2 and accused no.1 could not be secured, the case was split up and in the original case i.e. CC No.1/2013 the proceedings continued against accused nos.3 and 4 and against accused nos.1 and 2, the case was renumbered as CC No.281/2017. Aggrieved by the learned Magistrate taking cognizance of the offences 3 and issuing summons against the petitioner herein, the instant petition is filed.

2. Subsequent to filing of the petition, CC No.1/2013 has been decided and it has resulted in discharge of accused nos.3 and 4. In the process, the learned Magistrate has observed that the complainant has failed to satisfy by way of leading evidence that there are necessary ingredients of Sections 384 and 499 of IPC punishable under Section 500 of IPC and on the said ground, accused nos.3 and 4 are discharged. It is contended on behalf of the petitioner that accused nos.3 and 4 are discharged on the ground that the complainant i.e. respondent has failed to establish the fact of extortion or defamation as against all the persons concerned and not merely against accused nos.3 and 4 and for that reason, the proceedings against the petitioner herein needs to be quashed.

3. Per contra, the respondent submits that the decision of the trial court in C.C.No.1/2013 has not attained finality and a criminal revision petition is filed against the said order which is pending consideration. It is also alleged that the 4 material on record has been examined by the Magistrate only with a view to find out whether accused nos.3 and 4 are guilty or not and the evidence let in relating to CC No.1/2013 has not been examined from the fact whether accused nos.1 and 2 are guilty or not. It is also submitted that the evidence was let in only in respect of commissioning of the offence by accused nos.3 and 4 and not accused nos.1 and 2 and on the said grounds, it is contended that mere discharge of accused nos.3 and 4 does not entitle accused no.2 i.e. petitioner herein to seek quashment of criminal proceedings against him in C.C.No.281/2017.

4. Admittedly, a video clip was aired in TV 9 channel and it contained the respondent and his wife travelling on a motor bike and it is alleged that the said video was part of a news item that, there were blue films and certain illegal activities taking place in Mangaluru. Whether it constitutes defamation or not is a matter to be decided by the trial court based on the material available on record. Further, whether there was extortion or not also is a matter to be 5 decided by the trial court based on the material available on record. Further, whether petitioner herein was responsible for airing the said video or was involved in the alleged extortion also is a matter to be decided by the trial court based on the material available on record. It involves disputed question of facts and this Court while exercising its powers under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. cannot decide the same.

5. For the aforementioned reasons, the criminal petition is hereby dismissed. It is needless to state that the petitioner is always at liberty to work out all his remedies before the trial court including the application for discharge.

In view of dismissal of the petition, I.A.No.1/2018 does not survive for consideration and it stands disposed of.

SD/-

case_summary: In S.R. Parthiban vs The District Public Prosecutor, the petitioner, a sitting MLA of the Mettur Constituency, sought to quash criminal proceedings in C.C. No. 3 of 2019 before the Principal District and Sessions Judge, Salem. The case was based on allegations that the petitioner delivered a derogatory and defamatory speech against the then Chief Minister, Dr. J. Jayalalitha, during a political demonstration on 11.08.2015. The Tamil Nadu government had initially sanctioned the prosecution under Section 499 IPC, punishable under Section 500 IPC, but later issued a Government Order (G.O. Ms. No. 630) in 2021 to withdraw the case.
case_decision:
The Court held that the alleged speech was political criticism aimed at the Chief Minister in her personal capacity, rather than defamatory remarks related to her discharge of public duties. For a defamation case under Section 199(2) and 199(4) of CrPC to proceed, there must be a direct connection between the alleged imputation and the public functions of the individual. In this case, the Court found no such nexus, emphasizing that criticism of a political figure in their personal capacity does not warrant state prosecution. Instead, the remedy lies in a private complaint under Section 199(6) CrPC.
Citing K.K. Mishra vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh and Kartar Singh vs. State of Punjab, the Court noted that the use of state machinery to initiate defamation proceedings is inappropriate when the statements pertain to personal matters. Given the subsequent Government Order withdrawing prosecution, the Court deemed the case an abuse of process and quashed the proceedings.

case_summary: In V. Mullaivendhan vs The District Public Prosecutor, the petitioner, a former Minister, sought to quash criminal proceedings in C.C. No. 49 of 2018 before the Special Court of Trial for Criminal Cases related to elected members of Parliament and the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly. The proceedings stemmed from a political speech delivered by the petitioner during a demonstration on 30.09.2015, in which derogatory remarks were allegedly made against the then Chief Minister, Dr. J. Jayalalitha. The Tamil Nadu Government had sanctioned prosecution under Section 499 IPC, punishable under Section 500 IPC, but the petitioner contended that the remarks did not amount to defamation in the context of the Chief Minister's public duties.
case_decision:
The Court held that the alleged remarks were political criticism directed at the Chief Minister in her personal capacity as a party leader and not in connection with her official duties. To sustain a defamation charge under Section 199(2) and 199(4) CrPC, there must be a direct nexus between the imputation and the discharge of public functions. In this case, the Court found no such connection, emphasizing that criticisms of a public figure's political actions do not warrant state prosecution and must be addressed through private complaints.
Citing K.K. Mishra vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh and Kartar Singh vs. State of Punjab, the Court reiterated that state machinery should not be used to pursue defamation claims related to personal remarks. Since the alleged defamatory remarks had no nexus with the discharge of official duties, the Court ruled that the pending proceedings constituted an abuse of the legal process and quashed the case.

                                                          ORDER

The Criminal Original Petition has been filed to call for the records relating to C.C.No.49 of 2018 on the file of the Special Court of Trial for Criminal cases related to elected members of Parliament and Members of State Legislative Assembly of Tamil Nadu, Singaravelar Maligai, Chennai and quash the same.

2. The petitioner was a Minister during 1996-2001. The complaint given by the District Public Prosecutor against the petitioner is that there was a demonstration held near Mechery, Salem District within the jurisdiction limit of Mechery Police Station, Salem, organized by the DMDK party on 30.09.2015 and in that demonstration meeting, the petitioner is alleged to have addressed the gathering and delivered derogatory and defamatory speech against the Government lead by the then Chief Minister Dr.J.Jayalalitha.

3. Mr.J.Bharathi Raja, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner would submit that the alleged speech stated to have been delivered by the petitioner in a political meeting noway amounts to defamation as against the then Chief Minister in discharge of her public duties. Even assuming such https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 2/9 Crl.O.P.No. 3170 of 2019 statements may be defamatory, but, then in the absence of the nexus between the same and the discharge of public duties of the office of the Chief Minister, the remedy under Section 199(2) and 199(4) of Cr.P.C., will not be available to the Chief Minister. At the most, it amounts only to a criticism by a political opponent and thereby, the petitioner can only be prosecuted under Section 500 of IPC personally by her and not through the Public Prosecutor. However, based on G.O.Ms.No.146, dated 05.02.2016 issued by the Public (Law & Order-H) Department, the Government of Tamil Nadu had accorded sanction to the Respondent to prosecute the petitioner for the offence under Section 499 IPC, punishable under Section 500 IPC. In such circumstances, the prosecution as against the petitioner is nothing but an abuse of process of law and thereby he would seek for quashing the proceedings.

4. The learned Additional Public Prosecutor would submit that whether the statement delivered during the speech is of the defamative imputation and whether it caused damage to the public authorities or State or in personal capacity is a matter for trial and it cannot be decided at this stage in a quash petition.

https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 3/9 Crl.O.P.No. 3170 of 2019

5. Heard the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner and the learned Additional Public Prosecutor appearing for the respondent and perused the materials available on record.

6. It is contented by the counsel for the petitioner that to constitute an offence under Section 500 IPC against the Constitutional functionaries or the Minister or Chief Minister of State, it has to be established by the prosecution that the alleged imputation made is in respect of the conduct of the public servant/ public functionary in discharge of his/her public functions and the public functions stand on a different footing than the private activities of a public servant. If the statement made appears to be the criticism with regard to the political activities of a person in personal capacity, the right is guaranteed to the petitioner under Article 21 of the Constitution of India and further the complaint can be filed only in the personal capacity before the Court of Magistrate and state machinery cannot be used to initiate proceedings.

7. At this juncture, it is relevant to refer to the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in K.K.Mishra Vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh reported in (2018) 6 SCC 676, where in the Hon'ble Apex Court has held as follows:-

https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 4/9 Crl.O.P.No. 3170 of 2019
11. .... Such statements may be defamatory but then in the absence of a nexus between the same and the discharge of public duties of the office, the remedy Under Section 199(2) and 199(4) Code of Criminal Procedure will not be available. It is the remedy saved by the provisions of Sub-

section (6) of Section 199 Code of Criminal Procedure i.e. a complaint by the Hon'ble Chief Minister before the ordinary Court i.e. the Court of Magistrate which would be available and could have been resorted to.

case_summary: In R.S. Bharathi vs. City Public Prosecutor, the petitioner, a political leader, was accused of delivering a derogatory speech against the then Chief Minister, Dr. J. Jayalalitha, during a public meeting in 2015. The prosecution was initiated based on a Government Order sanctioning action under Section 499 IPC, punishable under Section 500 IPC. The petitioner argued that the speech amounted to political criticism rather than defamation in the discharge of public duties. Citing constitutional rights to free speech and the absence of a direct connection between the alleged defamation and the Chief Minister's official functions, the petitioner sought to quash the proceedings.
case_decision: The Madras High Court held that the alleged remarks were political criticism targeting the Chief Minister in her personal capacity as a party leader, not related to her public functions. The Court ruled that for defamation claims under Section 199(2) CrPC to proceed, the defamatory statements must relate directly to the public duties of the officeholder. Since the alleged remarks had no such nexus, the Court found the prosecution an abuse of legal process and quashed the proceedings, considering a subsequent Government Order directing withdrawal of the case.

Author: A.D.Jagadish Chandira

Bench: A.D.Jagadish Chandira

                                                                                Crl.O.P.No.7266 of 2021



                                  IN THE HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT MADRAS

                                                 DATED : 11.03.2022

                                                         CORAM :

                      THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE A.D.JAGADISH CHANDIRA

                                              Crl.O.P.No.7266 of 2021

                City Civil Court Buildings,
                Chennai – 600 104.                                              ... Respondent

                Procedure Code, pleased to call for the records in C.C.No.36 of 2016 on the file
                of the Hon'ble Special Court for Trail of Cases related to Members of
                Parliament and Members of Legislative Assembly of Tamil Nadu, Chennai and
                quash the same in the interest of justice.

                                        For Respondent      : Mr.A.Gokulakrishnan

                                                           ORDER

The Criminal Original Petition has been filed to call for the records in C.C.No.36 of 2016 on the file of the Hon'ble Special Court for Trail of Cases related to Members of Parliament and Members of Legislative Assembly of Tamil Nadu, Chennai and quash the same.

2. The complaint given by the City Public Prosecutor against the petitioner is that the petitioner is that there was a public meeting held within the jurisdiction limit of J-7, Velachery Police Station at Gandhi Salai, organized by South Madras Youth Wing on 02.11.2015 from 19.00 hours to 22.00 hours and in that public meeting, the petitioner had delivered a derogatory and defamatory speech against the Government lead by the then Chief Minister Dr.J.Jayalalitha.

3. Mr.S.Manuraj, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner would submit that the alleged speech stated to have been delivered by the petitioner in a political meeting noway amounts to defamation as against the then Chief Minister in discharge of her public duties. Even assuming such statements may be defamatory, but, then in the absence of the nexus between the same and the discharge of public duties of the office of the Chief Minister, the remedy under https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 2/8 Crl.O.P.No.7266 of 2021 Section 199(2) and 199(4) of Cr.P.C., will not be available to the Chief Minister. At the most, it amounts only to a criticism by a political opponent and thereby, the petitioner can only be prosecuted under Section 500 of IPC personally by her and not through the Public Prosecutor. Further, the Tamil Nadu Government by G.O.Ms.No.235, dated 01.03.2016 issued by the Public (Law & Order-H) department, had accorded sanction to the Respondent to prosecute the petitioner for the offence under Section 499 IPC, punishable under Section 500 IPC. Subsequently, the Government by a later G.O.Ms.No.560 dated 10.08.2021 issued by the Public (Law & Order-H) department has directed withdrawal of prosecutions from the above said case and also dropped the further action in the above said case. In such circumstances, the prosecution as against the petitioner is nothing but an abuse of process of law and thereby he would seek for quashing the proceedings.

4. The learned Additional Public Prosecutor would submit that whether the statement delivered during the speech is of the defamative imputation and whether it caused damage to the public authorities or State or in personal capacity is a matter for trial and it cannot be decided at this stage in a quash petition. However, he would admit that the Government had issued a G.O.Ms.No.560 dated 10.08.2021, directing the Public Prosecutor to withdraw the case against the petitioner.

https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 3/8 Crl.O.P.No.7266 of 2021

5. Heard the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner and the learned Additional Public Prosecutor appearing for the respondent and perused the materials available on record including the transcript of the alleged defamatory speech.

6. It is contented by the counsel for the petitioner that to constitute an offence under Section 500 IPC against the Constitutional functionaries or the Minister or Chief Minister of State, it has to be established by the prosecution that the alleged imputation made is in respect of the conduct of the public servant/ public functionary in discharge of his/her public functions and the public functions stand on a different footing than the private activities of a public servant. If the statement made appears to be the criticism with regard to the political activities of a person in personal capacity, the right is guaranteed to the petitioner under Article 21 of the Constitution of India and further the complaint can be filed only in the personal capacity before the Court of Magistrate and state machinery cannot be used to initiate proceedings.

7. At this juncture, it is relevant to refer to the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in K.K.Mishra Vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 4/8 Crl.O.P.No.7266 of 2021 reported in (2018) 6 SCC 676, where in the Hon'ble Apex Court has held as follows:-

11. .... Such statements may be defamatory but then in the absence of a nexus between the same and the discharge of public duties of the office, the remedy Under Section 199(2) and 199(4) Code of Criminal Procedure will not be available. It is the remedy saved by the provisions of Sub-

section (6) of Section 199 Code of Criminal Procedure i.e. a complaint by the Hon'ble Chief Minister before the ordinary Court i.e. the Court of Magistrate which would be available and could have been resorted to.

8. Similarly, in Kartar Singh Vs. State of Punjab reported in AIR 1956 SC 541, the Hon'ble Apex Court has held that vulgar abuses made against the public functionaries will not amount to defamation of the State but may amount only to the defamation of the public functionaries concerned and therefore, they are only personal in nature. The Hon'ble Apex Court, though finding that the slogans were certainly defamatory of the public functionaries, hax held that the redress of that grievance was personal to the individuals and state machinery cannot be used to initiate the proceedings. https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 5/8 Crl.O.P.No.7266 of 2021

9. This Court, having meticulously perused the transcript of the speech alleged to have been delivered by the petitioner, is of the considered opinion that it is only a political criticism on the then Chief Minister in her personal capacity and by no stretch of imagination, it would amount to defamation against the then Chief Minister in discharge of her official functions.

10. As state above, to take cognizance of the complaint under Section 199(2) of Cr.P.C, the so called defamation should be directly attributed to a person in discharge of his/her public functions and only in such circumstances, Section 199(2) of Cr.P.C will stand attracted. If the said imputation apparently made against the public functionaries, has no nexus with the discharge of public duties, the remedy available under Section 199(6) of Cr.P.C is only to make private complaint before the regular Magistrate and the remedy under Section 199(2) and 199(4) will not be available. Otherwise, if any criticism or defamation in the nature of personal capacity and such defamation have no nexus with the discharge of official function of public functionaries of the state, complaint cannot be made by the Public Prosecutor merely on the basis of Government Order.

https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 6/8 Crl.O.P.No.7266 of 2021

11. In view of the foregoing reasons and the decisions cited supra, and also in view of the subsequent Government Order dated 10.08.2021 directing withdrawal of prosecution, this Court is of the opinion that the pending proceedings in C.C.No.36 of 2016, on the file of the Hon'ble Special Court for Trail of Cases related to Members of Parliament and Members of Legislative Assembly of Tamil Nadu, Chennai, is only an abuse of process of law and the proceedings are quashed.

12. Accordingly, the Criminal Original Petition stands allowed. Consequently, connected miscellaneous petition is closed.

https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Section 199(2) and 199(4) of Cr.P.C., will not be available to the Chief
Minister. At the most, it amounts only to a criticism by a political opponent and
thereby, the petitioner can only be prosecuted under Section 500 of IPC
personally by her and not through the Public Prosecutor. Further, the Tamil
Nadu Government by G.O.Ms.No.235, dated 01.03.2016 issued by the Public
(Law & Order-H) department, had accorded sanction to the Respondent to
prosecute the petitioner for the offence under Section 499 IPC, punishable
under Section 500 IPC. Subsequently, the Government by a later
G.O.Ms.No.560 dated 10.08.2021 issued by the Public (Law & Order-H)
department has directed withdrawal of prosecutions from the above said case
and also dropped the further action in the above said case. In such
circumstances, the prosecution as against the petitioner is nothing but an abuse
of process of law and thereby he would seek for quashing the proceedings.
This Court, having meticulously perused the transcript of the
speech alleged to have been delivered by the petitioner, is of the considered
opinion that it is only a political criticism on the then Chief Minister in her
personal capacity and by no stretch of imagination, it would amount to
defamation against the then Chief Minister in discharge of her official
functions.
conclusion:

In view of the foregoing reasons and the decisions cited supra,
and also in view of the subsequent Government Order dated 10.08.2021
directing withdrawal of prosecution, this Court is of the opinion that the
pending proceedings in C.C.No.36 of 2016, on the file of the Hon'ble Special
Court for Trail of Cases related to Members of Parliament and Members of
Legislative Assembly of Tamil Nadu, Chennai, is only an abuse of process of
law and the proceedings are quashed.

case_summary: In M/S BTM First Grade College vs. K.N. Shanth Kumar, the complainant, BTM First Grade College, alleged that the defendant, K.N. Shanth Kumar, the editor of the Kannada newspaper Prajavani, published a defamatory article on May 25, 2017, claiming the college did not meet required standards. The complainant contended that the article caused reputational and financial harm, leading to decreased student enrollment. The complainant sought compensation for defamation under Sections 500, 501, and 502 of the IPC. The defendant argued that the article was based on official reports from the Bangalore University Local Inquiry Committee and was published in good faith as a matter of public concern.
case_decision: The court acquitted the defendant, ruling that the article was based on true and publicly available documents, such as the inquiry report and syndicate meeting proceedings. The court found no evidence of malice or intent to defame, and since the publication was a fair report of public interest, it fell under the exceptions of Section 499 IPC. Thus, the complainant failed to prove the elements of defamation, and the defendant was found not guilty of the charges.

       This is a private complaint filed by the Complainant

       2. The brief facts of the case is as under :

       It is the case of Complainant that the Complainant is

University Syndicate and even without taking any decision

in regard to any of the education institution at Bengaluru,

the accused being Editor of Prajavani        daily news paper

has published an article and spread wrong message to the

general public on 25.05.2017 as ಬ.ಟ.ಎಎ ಪ ಪಥಮ ದರರ ಖಸಗ

     3.   It is further case of Complainant that on

perusing publication of accused, Bengaluru University has

the Registrar of Bengaluru University to place records of

     4.   It is further case of complainant that thereafter

the State Government has renewed the       permission and

affiliation to run the education institution vide its order

dated 08.08.2018.    Accused displayed and published a

false information in its newspaper and caused great social
                                              CC No. 25649 /2018
                                 5

stigma, de­reputation to Complainant education Institution

in the society and also caused financial loss to the

Complainant.     The   said    news   articles   published    on

25.05.2017 and caused great loss and damage to the

institution to run the institution in smooth manner

because of that false news, the number of students/pupils

have left the college by receiving their deposits and their

caused a great financial loss to the complainant and also

Complainant that the Complainant has faced multiple

which is punishable U/s 500, 501 IPC.

     5.   It    is   further   case   of   Complainant       that

Complainant issued notice to the accused and said notice

was duly served. Inspite of it accused has not clarified the
                                                  CC No. 25649 /2018
                                  6

matter nor published the clarification in the news paper

and thereby accused has committed the offence. Accused

has defamed the name of Complainant, Educational

Institution and also caused financial loss and caused

damage to institution for smooth running of institution. As

such        accused is liable to pay           compensation      of

Rs.25,00,000/­ to the Complainant Education Society and

also    Rs.50,000/­     towards       legal    charges    to   the

Complainant.



       6.    After registering the Complaint, this Court has

recorded     the   Sworn   Statement      of   Complainant     and

thereafter has taken the cognizance for the offences U/s

500, 501, 502 of I.P.C and registered the case as CC and

issued summons to the accused.



       7.    In pursuance to summons, accused            appeared

through his counsel and he is on Court bail.
                                           CC No. 25649 /2018
                               7

     8.    Thereafter, the Complainant has produced the

list of witness and examined one K.N.Ramesh who is the

then Principal of the said college as CW­2. The Sworn

Statement of Complainant was treated as evidence before

charge as prayed by the Complainant through memo and

no fresh evidence was lead by CW­1. Thereafter, charge

was framed against the accused for which he pleaded not

guilty and claims to be tried. Again, Ld.counsel for

Complainant has adopted the Sworn Statement evidence

as his evidence and got marked Ex.C­1 to 8. During the

course    of   cross­examination   some   documents    were

confronted to the witness on behalf of the accused and

they were marked as Ex.D­1 to 6. Accused has not lead

any oral evidence.



     9.    Heard the arguments. Perused the documents

placed on record.
                                               CC No. 25649 /2018
                                  8

        10. The following points that arise for consideration
is :
          1. Whether the Complainant proves beyond
          all reasonable doubt that accused has
          committed an offences punishable U/s 500,
          501 and 502 of I.P.C ?

          2. What order ?


       11. The above points are answered as under :
             Point No.1: In the Negative.
             Point No.2: As per final order for the following :
                         REASONS


        12. Point No.1 :    It is the case of Complainant that

accused has published a defamatory article in the news

article in his paper dated 25.05.2017, due to which

Complainant Institution sustained loss and the name of

Complainant Institution was defammed. After appearance

of accused, accused denied the case of Complainant and

his defence is that he has published the news article dated

25.05.2017 based on the documents i.e, Ex.D­3 to 5 the

proceedings of Syndicate meetings of Bengaluru University
                                           CC No. 25649 /2018
                               9

was uploaded and based on that news he published the

news and the subject matter of publication i.e., news

article published on 25.05.2017 relates to the decision

taken by Syndicate held in the       sub meeting held on

25.04.2017 with regard to non­renewal of affiliation of

Complainant's college and the accused being news paper

has brought the notice of       general public as to what

transpired in the LIC report and Syndicate meeting since it

is a matter of    public importance and the news article

published on     25.05.2017   pertains to the importance of

public concern and the publication is true and faithful

report of fact. Therefore, accused has not committed any

offence etc.,

     13.   The Complainant in order to substantiate      its

case one Srinivas is examined as CW­1/PW­1 and he has

reiterated the complaint averments in detail on oath. On

behalf of Complainant one witness one Ramesh K.N who is

the then principal of said BTM College is examined as CW­

2 on behalf of Complainant 07 documents i.e, CW­1 to7
                                            CC No. 25649 /2018
                               10

are marked. Ex.C­1 is the copy of the communication

issued by Prl. Secretary to the Secretary BTM COllege for

grant of affliation for the academic year 2006­07. Ex.C­2 is

the copy of notification issued by Bengaluru University for

renewal of affiliation for the academic year 2016­17. Ex.C­

3 is the copy of registration certificate of Srinivas

Educational Society Ex.C­4 is the copy of news paper

article dated 25.05.2017. Ex.C­5 is the show­cause notice

issued to Complainant College, Bengaluru University Ex.C­

6 is the copy of Communication issued by Prl. Secretary to

Government. Ex.C­7 is the copy of Legal notice issued by

Complainant.

     14.   CW­1 and 2 were thoroughly cross­examined by

Ld.counsel for accused and during the cross­examination

some important points have been admitted by CW­1 and 2

which will be discussed later and they have denied other

material   suggestions.   During    the   course   of   cross­

examination some documents were confronted by defence

counsel and they are admitted by CW­1 and 2 and they
                                             CC No. 25649 /2018
                              11

got marked as Ex.D­1 to 6. Ex.D­1 is the copy of Order

passed by Hon'ble High Court in W.P.No.28463/2017 and

Ex.D­2 is the Order passed    in W.P.No.14928/2017 and

Ex.D­3 is the Local inquiry committee report Ex.D­4 is the

extract of the proceedings of Syndicate meetings of

academic counsel. Ex.D­5 is the extract of the special

meeting of Syndicate, Ex.D­6 is the copy of vice­chancellor

approval with respect of non­extension of affliation to BTM

First Grade College for the year 2017­18.

     15.   The Ld.consel for Complainat and accused in

addition to their oral arguments they also submitted their

written arguments and citations in support of their

contention. The main point canvassed by Complainant is

that the accused has published the defamtory article on

25.05.2017 without any basis and caused loss to the BTM

First Grade College and thereby committed the offences

punishable U/s 500, 501, 502 of I.P.C., and in support of

arguments the Ld.counsel for Complainant has relied upon

the following citations.
                                          CC No. 25649 /2018
                              12

1.    ILR 2021 KAR 835

     Selvina Kom Peter Byarko V/s Ganesh P and another

2.     ILR 2020 KAR 5143

        Smt.Sushma Rani V/s Sri.H.N.Nagaraja Rao

3.     Crl.CCC.No.1 of 2020 C/w dated 28.01.2020

       16.   On the other­hand the main contention of

accused is that he is the editor   of daily kannada news

paper namely Prajavani     and the article published on

25.05.2017 is based on the documents i.e., Local Inquiry

Report and the Syndicate meetings decision which was

held on 24.05.2017 and as per the local inquiry committee

report and the Syndicate Proceedings clearly reflected the

score obtained by the Complainant College as per Ex.D­5

and it is only 27­37% which is below 40% and lesser than

the minimum score fixed by the University and based on

that materials news was published. So, accused has not

committed any offence as alleged in the complaint. To

constitute the offence U/s 499 of IPC     there are some
                                           CC No. 25649 /2018
                               13

ingredients are to be proved by the      Complainant and

Complainant has not proved such ingredients which are

stated in Sec.499 IPC. There is no mensrea which is the

mandatory pre­requisite of offence    of defemation it    is

clearly missing in the present case and the news article

published on 25.05.2017 was based on public documents

and it is the duty of members to bring it to the knowledge

of publics as it is a matter of public importance. Since the

said news item pertains to matter of public concern and

publication is true and faithful report of fact. It comes

under the first exception   of Sec.499 of IPC which was

published in good faith. Therefore, the publication of news

article dated 25.05.2017 clearly falls within the ambit of

first exception to Sec.499 and it is based on the public

documents and article was reported as per the materials

and true facts as to what transpired         in   Syndicate

meetings and Local inquiry Committe report in the interest

of general public. Therefore, accused has not at all
                                            CC No. 25649 /2018
                               14

committed any offences. In support of his contention

accused counsel has relied upon the following decisions :

1.   R.Krishnamurthy & Others V/s A.Nandhini 200

     SCC Online Mad 11883.

2.   Grievances Redressal Officer and Others against

     V.V.MInerals Pvt. Ltd., dated 05.05.2020

3.   The Karnataka State Universities Act, 2000.

     17.   In the light of the above submission and

arguments and materials available on record once again I

have carefully perused the entire evidence available on

record. The main allegation of Complainant is that the

accused without any basis has published the news article

and defammed the name of Complainant college. Due           to

the said publishing of article the college has sustained loss

etc. As discussed above the Complainant             adduced

evidence and CW­1 has reiterated the complaint averments

in detail in his evidence.   During the cross­examination

CW­1 has    admitted that affairs of Education Institution
                                            CC No. 25649 /2018
                               15

are subjected to the interest of public and he further stated

due to said publishing of article the college was sustained

loss but during the cross­examination vaguly stated that 5

to 6 students have taken their Transfer Certificate from the

college pursuant to the publication. But to fortify the said

contention or to substantiate the said contention he has

not placed any documentary evidence before the Court. If

really due to the publication of news article College was

sustained loss or any other damage he could have placed

some materials before the Court. As rightly pointed out by

the Ld.counsel for accused the evidence placed by

Complainant in that regard his vague and no specific

evidence   is placed before the Court which cannot be

accepted. Further, CW­1 during the course of his evidence

has stated he does not remember how many students

admitted for the academic year 2018­2019 and no

documents are produced in that regard it also creates

doubt regarding the case of Complainant. If really       the

publication was caused damage to the college and due to
                                                CC No. 25649 /2018
                                 16

which some reduction in admission etc., he would have

placed some materials before the Court. Admittedly no

such materials are placed before the Court. When such

being the case the contention of the Complainant that he

has sustained financial loss etc, cannot be accepted. He

further   admitted   during    the    course    of   his   cross­

examination that the defects pointed out in Ex.C­6 were

rectified in the year 2019­20. So, it clearly establishes the

Local committee report is correct and based on that report

news article was published by accused and subsequently

the said defects were rectified as per the admission of CW­

1. So, it is crystal clear at the time of local inquiry

committee inspection there was some defects in the College

and the Committee was noted down the said defects and

submitted to the       Syndicate counsel and Syndicate

members. Considering the said report Syndicate members

have taken some action.       When such being the case the

Complainant cannot contended that only on publication of

article on   25.05.2017       by accused, there was some
                                                CC No. 25649 /2018
                                 17

reduction     in admission and College was sustained loss

etc.

       18.   Further, CW­2 who is the then          Principal of

Complainant College has admitted during the inspection

by LIC they have taken videograph and CD was handed

over to him and it was not produced before the Court.

Further, he also admitted the building was in dilapidated

condition and he was also physically present when LIC was

inspected the spot for      grant of affiliation. He further

admits report of proceedings was sent to the Complainant

College.

       19.   On perusal of evidence of CW­2 it also clearly

indicates that there was some defects in the College         and

LIC has inspected the College and given the report. Based

on the report the Syndicate members have taken some

decision and issued Show­cause notice to the Complainant

college.

       20.   On   perusal   of   Ex.D­1   it     discloses   the

Complainant College has challenged the Show­cause notice
                                                  CC No. 25649 /2018
                                  18

issued by Vice­chancellor, Bengaluru University. Based on

the Syndicate meetings and the said Show­cause notice

was rejected and the Hon'ble High Court has directed the

2nd Respondent in the said Writ Petition i.e., Vice

Chancellor,      Bengaluru   University    to    constitute   legal

inspection     Committee      consisting    of      faculty   wise

Sr.Professors and complete the exercise of consideration of

the application for renewal of affiliation within a period of

six weeks from today and disposed the writ petition.

     21.     Ex.D­3 discloses that the local inquiry committe

has inspected the BTM first grade College i.e., Complainant

College. On      22.04.2017 and noted some defects in the

College and the Committee has given marks to the said

College    and     total   weightage   score     obtained       by

Complainant College was 27.37%. As per the parameter

minimum percentage of score was assigned for renewal of

affiliation is 40%. The said Complainant BTM College has

obtained only 27.37% which is lesser than 40%. Ex.D­4 is

the Special meeting of academic counsel               proceedings
                                              CC No. 25649 /2018
                                   19

which was held on         22.05.2017 and in item No.4 in the

said proceedings is inrespect of Complainant College

wherein it is held that the Chairperson of LIC has clarified

that the facilities in the College are inadequate and detailed

observations have been made about the infrastructure.

Therefore, the Committee has not recommended for

renewal of affiliation. However, the house can take the a

decision in this regard after detailed discussion and the

house resolved to recommend for re­inspection of College

by another committee.

     22.   From     the     said   observation   of   meetings

proceedings it is crystal clear the local committee        has

visited the spot and clearly noted the defects and facilities

available in the College and not recommended for renewal

of affiliation.   Ex.D­5 is also the meetings proceedings

which was held on            24.05.2017. Wherein, also the

Syndicate members of Bengaluru University have taken the

decision that not to recommend the renewal of affiliation to

the said college and said college was obtained score to the
                                              CC No. 25649 /2018
                                  20

extent of 27.37%. Ex.D­6 is the copy of Chancellor

approval with respect to non­extension of        affiliation to

BTM College for the year 2017­18 and it clearly shows the

Complainant College was not eligible for renewal of

affiliation and show­cause notice was issued to the said

College.   All   these   Ex.D­3   to   6   documents    clearly

establishes that the local committee has inspected the

College and submitted report and as per the report the

score obtained by Complainant College is only 27.37%

which is less than        minimum score, for renewal of

affiliation minimum score is 40%. Based on that report

Syndicate members decided to issue show­cause notice

and issued show­cause notice to the Complainant College.

So, all these documents       clearly establishes there was

some defects in the college at the time of institution and

based on the said report and materials the accused paper

has published the report. Therefore, this Court is of the

opinion that the accused has not at all committed any

offence as alleged by the Complainant.             As rightly
                                           CC No. 25649 /2018
                               21

contended by Ld.counsel for accused it is the duty of

accused to bring it to the knowledge of the general public.

As the said news or article is a matter of public

importance.

     23.   Further,   during   the   course   of   argument

Ld.counsel for complainant has mainly canvassed his

arguments that due to publishing of said news article,

college has sustained    loss and there was reduction in

admissions and due to that news article is social stigma

and dereputation in the society was caused to the

complainant which cannot be compensated in terms of

money. However, for such loss and defamation accused is

liable to pay compensation to the tune of Rs.25,00,000/­

and prays to award the same.

     24.   Again in the light of above arguments,    I have

carefully perused the evidence onceagain. As discussed

above except some vague evidence in respect of alleged loss

Complainant has not placed any evidence before the Court.

Even with regard to alleged defamation or reduction of
                                            CC No. 25649 /2018
                               22

admissions and with regard to alleged stigma on the college

and dereputation etc., there is no material is placed by the

Complainant. As discussed above accused has published

the said news based on the documentary evidence when

there is defect in the college the question of defaming the

Complainant college would not arise at all. As rightly

pointed out by Ld.counsel for accused it is the duty of

accused being news paper editor to bring the true facts to

the knowledge of general public as the said matter is of

public importance.     Thus   it is clear that there is no

mensrea on the part of accused in the said publication of

news article dated 25.05.2017.      It is one of   the most

essential ingredient that there must be mensrea which is

absent in the present case and it is clearly missing in the

case.   Since, the      publication of news item dated

25.05.2017 inrespect of Complainant college pertains to

matter of public concern and the publication is based on

true facts and reports of      concerned committee, the

question of   defamation or degrading the reputation of
                                           CC No. 25649 /2018
                               23

complainant college   as contended by the Ld.counsel for

complainant would not arise at all and the contention of

Ld.counsel for Complainant that a false report was

published and due to which the reputation of college was

degraded etc., is not acceptable one.

     25.   I have gone through the decision   relied by the

Ld.counsel for the Complainant. The Hon'ble High Court

case_summary: The case involved a defamation complaint filed by the Murasoli Trust against Dr. S. Ramadoss, a political leader, in response to several tweets made by him on his official Twitter account. The tweets suggested that the Trust occupied "Panchami land" (land originally allotted to members of Scheduled Castes) without legitimate ownership. Dr. Ramadoss had questioned the legality of the land's ownership and demanded that the Trust present original title deeds. Despite the Trust's denial and response, Dr. Ramadoss continued to tweet about the issue, prompting the Trust to file a defamation complaint under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The Trust claimed that the tweets caused mental agony, degraded its reputation, and sought a legal remedy for defamation.
case_decision: The Madras High Court quashed the defamation complaint against Dr. S. Ramadoss. It ruled that the tweets were framed as questions about the land's ownership and did not contain any statements that could be considered defamatory. The court emphasized that to establish defamation, there must be a clear intent to harm the reputation of the complainant, which was not evident in this case. The court also noted that Dr. Ramadoss’s questions fell under the exceptions to defamation outlined in Section 499 IPC and were not intended to harm the Trust's reputation but were part of a political dialogue. Therefore, the complaint was dismissed as it lacked prima facie evidence of defamation.

2. The respondent filed private complaint for the offences punishable under Sections 499 & 500 of IPC. The crux of the allegations in the complaint is that the respondent owns, prints and publishes the daily newspaper Murasoli. The petitioner is the founder of a political party and he manages a twitter handle under the name and style of Dr.S.Ramadoss with URL http://twitter.com/drramadoss (hereinafter after called as “official twitter account”). The petitioner twitted from his official twitter account on 17.10.2019. Further he also twitted four twits from his official twitter account on 19.10.2019 at about 12.07 p.m. Once again he twitted from his official twitter account on 19.11.2019 at 8.39 p.m. https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Page 2 of 22 Crl.O.P.No.6763 of 2020

3. According to the respondent, the contents of the twits are false, baseless, untrue and per se defamatory. It constitutes a calculated attempt to malign the reputation of the respondent. The constitutional protection of freedom of speech and expression is subject to reasonable restrictions, which includes defamation as such, the action of the petitioner falls beyond the scope of freedom of speech. He is seeking political mileage and his ulterior motive is apparent from the twits made by him against the respondent's political party. There is no bona fide reason for raising this issue by way of twitter. Therefore, the respondent has suffered immeasurable mental agony and the reputation of the Murasoli Trust has been degraded, tarnished and smeared due to the twits made by the petitioner.

4. Therefore, the respondent caused legal notice dated 22.11.2019, thereby called upon the petitioner to remove the above defamatory twits dated 17.10.2019, 19.10.2019 & 19.11.2019. Further tender an open and unconditional apology within 48 hours from the date of receipt of the notice and refrain from repeating such unethical acts in future. After receipt of the same, the petitioner issued reply notice containing untrue and defamatory statement. Hence the respondent https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Page 3 of 22 Crl.O.P.No.6763 of 2020 lodged the present complaint. On receipt of the complaint, the trial Court had taken cognizance in C.C.No.1280 of 2020 for the offences punishable under Sections 499 & 500 of IPC and issued summons to the petitioner.

5. The learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner submitted that the complaint filed by the respondent is not at all maintainable under penal law, since the trust has no right to question the twits made by the petitioner. The trust is not a legal entity to make a complaint for defamation before the Court of law. The petitioner being the founder and leader of the political party, relentlessly fighting for securing social justice for all section of people and to eradicate poverty to provide free education for children and to eliminate corruption from public life and politics. He is the one to critically analyze the policies, acts and deed of the Governments in power and of various organizations in public domain including political parties and makes unbiased, impartial and constructive comments on the functioning of such entities in the larger interest of and the welfare of citizens of the country. https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Page 4 of 22 Crl.O.P.No.6763 of 2020 5.1. He further submitted that the rival political party leader had seen a Tamil movie “Asuran” and had twitted that the film is not a movie, but a lesson. Therefore, the petitioner had twitted that he believed that the panchami land has to be returned by the respondent trust by learning lesson from the said movie, since there has been a consistent demand from many organizations and political parties to restore panchami land from the respondent trust to its lawful owners. After the twit, the respondent's political party leader had shown the patta copy of the respondent trust in support of his claim. By way of reply, the petitioner has twitted that the patta copy is not a title document and made a demand to show the title deed and parent document related to the respondent. Though the respondent's political party leader replied that where ever it required, it will be produced at appropriate time before the suitable forum, he did not come forward to produce any title deed as promised by him. Therefore, there is no defamatory words in the twits made by the petitioner.

5.2. He further submitted that on the complaint before the National Commission for SC & ST, the respondent was issued with notice. The said notice was challenged before this Court in W.P.No.35 of https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Page 5 of 22 Crl.O.P.No.6763 of 2020 2020. In the said writ petition, the respondent categorically stated that they are tenant and not owner of the property. They are the tenant of the punjami land which belongs to one Anjugammal Trust. Therefore, the present complaint is nothing but clear abuse of process of law and liable to be quashed.

5.3. He also submitted that the said issue was raised by various political parties including the person belongs to the same political party of the respondent. In fact, the current Minister who is holding Cabinet rank also made statement about the land in which the respondent trust is situated. However the respondent picked the petitioner alone and lodged the complaint. Further the petitioner never made any statement to defame the respondent or its political party. The petitioner raised question and it would not amount to defamation and it comes under the first exception of Section 499 of IPC. In support of his contention, he relied upon the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India reported in 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1434 in the case of Manoj Kumar Tiwari Vs. Manish Sisodia & ors.

https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Page 6 of 22 Crl.O.P.No.6763 of 2020

6. Per contra, the respondent filed counter and the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent submitted that the petitioner made totally seven twits thereby defamed the reputation of the respondent trust and its political party. The defamatory twits are false, baseless, untrue and per se defamatory. It is individual and severally constitute a calculated attempt to malign the reputation of the respondent. Therefore, immediately the respondent caused legal notice and even after receipt of the same, the petitioner failed to remove the twits made by him. The respondent is an aggrieved party due to the defamatory twits made by the petitioner and as such, it has locus standi and the present complaint is very must maintainable. It cannot be alleged that the compliant is made against the petitioner for political reason. On plain reading of the twits prima facie constitute the offence of defamation. It was made with ulterior motive only to defame the respondent.

6.1. He further submitted that on the complaint before the National Commission for SC & ST, the respondent produced all the original documents pertaining to the respondent and the same was duly verified by then Vice Chairperson of the Commission for SC & ST, New https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Page 7 of 22 Crl.O.P.No.6763 of 2020 Delhi. However, the said Vice Chairperson has become a Minister and made a statement thereby defamed the respondent trust. Hence the respondent trust filed complaint in C.C.No.47 of 2021 on the file of the learned Assistant Sessions Judge/Additional Special Court for Trial of Cases related to MP&MLA, Chennai and the same was challenged before this Court in Crl.O.P.No.10277 of 2022. This Court by an order dated 05.09.2023, dismissed the quash petition. The very same defamatory statement made by him, is now made by the petitioner herein.

6.2. While dismissing the quash petition, this Court observed that in an offence of defamation, the statement have to be tested only from the point of view of a common prudent man, who comes across the defamatory statements made. Even if the petitioner thinks that there was no imputation and that he had merely put a question, such statement will be understood by others as if the petitioner is repeatedly questioning the right and title of the property, over which the respondent trust is functioning and he also wants to drive home the point that it is functioning in the panchami land. That is how the respondent has understood the statements made by the petitioner and even in the complaint, the allegations have been made to the effect that many others https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis Page 8 of 22 Crl.O.P.No.6763 of 2020 had understood it in the same manner and started making enquiries with the respondent.

6.3. Therefore, this Court cannot go into the merits of the case of disputed questions of fact. It has to merely go by what is alleged in the complaint and prima facie find out as to whether the offence is made out. On going through the complaint and also the materials placed, this Court is prima facie convinced that the first limb of the offence of defamation has been satisfied by the complaint given against the petitioner. The petitioner also made similar twits with same set of allegation. Therefore, the respondent made out prima facie case to constitute the offence under Section 499 of IPC., and prayed for dismissal of the quash petition.

In the said issue the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India answered for the issue whether the twits attributed can be said to be per se defamatory and held as follows :-

61.
