facts:
The 2nd respondent filed a criminal complaint for the
offence under Sections 120-B , 499 , 500 & 502 of IPC against
the petitioners. In the said complaint, it is stated that the
complainant/2nd respondent herein is a successful
businessman and runs charitable organizations. On
03.2018, a scrolling was repeatedly shown on NTV( next
generation TV) regarding a person selling gutkha illegally,
would be shown. Thereafter on the next day on 17.03.2018, a program titled "Operation R.R.Gutka" was telecast on the A2/
NTV news channel, which was being run by A1company. The
duration of the said program was more than 10 minutes
which was repeatedly telecast. In the said news item it was
shown that the complainant in the name of R.R.Gutka was
selling poisonous substance which was banned. The news
reader referred to and addressed complainant as 'Mafia Don',
'Kanthiri', 'Ketugaadu', 'Kachodi', Paniki malina Bachaagadu',
'Old city Don', 'K.D', 'Durmargudu', 'Adda Gadidha' and
stated that he has amassed more than Rs.100 Crores at the
cost of public health. The news reader, who is A6 reported
that the complainant was running a Mafia Network in the Old
City and was very influential. It was further mentioned that
the complainant was associated with Dawood Ibrahim, a
notorious terrorist. News item also mentioned that the
complainant was a distributer of Goa Gutka and started
manufacturing duplicate Goa Gutka and when he was
confronted by Joshi, the owner and manager of 'Goa Gutka'
the complainant had sought the help of Dawood Ibrahim, who in turn threatened the said Joshi and ever since the
complainant became 'Hameed Bhai'.
Further, the property of the sons of the complaint which
was situated in Abids area was also shown on TV and
mentioned that illegal activities were going on in the said
complex. In the said broadcast, the complainant was branded
as an associate of terrorist namely Dawood Ibrahim and
mentioned that he was carrying out nefarious activities.
Further, the complainant was addressed in the most vulgar
and derogatory manner.
The complainant sent a legal notice on 19.03.2018
calling upon the petitioners/accused to issue unconditional
apology. However, no apology was sought by the accused and
neither apologized nor the conditions that were mentioned in
the legal notice were addressed.
issues:
Since the petitioners in all these petitions are seeking to
quash the proceedings arising out of CC No.236 of 2018 on
the file of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate at Hyderabad, they
are being heard together and disposed by way of this
Common Order.
Criminal Petition No.280 of 2022 is filed by the
petitioners/A1, A3 to A5, Criminal Petition No.11517 of 2022
is filed by A2 and Criminal Petition No.11536 of 2022 is filed
by A6 to A11in the calendar case.
pet_args:
Thereafter, aggrieved by taking cognizance against the
petitioners, petitioners filed Revision Petition No.175 of 2018
before the Hon'ble Sessions Judge, which was also dismissed.
Learned Sessions Judge found that the trial Court has rightly
taken cognizance against the accused. The telecast of news
branding the complainant as mafia don and using several
abusive words amounts to offence of defamation.
Sri T.Pradyumna Kumar Reddy, learned Senior counsel
appearing on behalf of Sri T.S.Anirudh Reddy, learned
counsel for the petitioners would submit that the allegations
made in the complaint do not make out any offence of
defamation. Admittedly, the police had raided the premises of
the complainant and during investigation it was found that
the complainant was involved in manufacturing banned
tobacco products. The cognizance taken by the learned
Magistrate is bad in law and accordingly, the proceedings
have to be quashed. In support of his contention, he relied on
the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of
Managing Director, Castrol India Limited v. State of
Karnataka and another [(2018) 17 Supreme Court Cases
275], wherein it is held as follows: " 5. A reading of the complaint petition in question does not
disclose that any specific act of the appellant resulted in
commission of the offences alleged. In the compounding notice
issued by the Inspector of Legal Metrology it has been mentioned
that the allegedly offending goods (Castrol Plus) were
manufactured plus packed by M/s. Castrol India Limited. The
offence, therefore, has been committed by the Company and the
appellant has been sought to be made vicariously liable merely
because at the relevant point of time he was holding the office of
Managing Director of Castrol India Limited."
In the result, the proceedings against the
petitioners/A1, A3 to A5 in C.C No.236 of 2018 on the file of
Chief Metropolitan Magistrate at Hyderabad, are hereby
quashed. Learned Senior Counsel alternatively argued that in
the event of this Court not finding favour with the grounds,
the attendance of the accused may be dispensed with. Accordingly, the attendance of A6 to A11 is dispensed subject
to the condition that the counsel proceeds with the trial in
their absence and subject to filing an affidavit by the
petitioners stating that in their absence the proceedings
conducted by their counsel will not be disputed by them in
any manner and also they shall not dispute their identity.
However, the petitioners shall appear before the learned
Magistrate as and when their presence is required. In the
event of the petitioners' failure to appear when the Court
directs, this order dispensing their attendance would stand
cancelled. The 2nd Accused can be represented by any
representative of the company in accordance with Section
of Cr.P.C.
resp_args:
On the other hand, learned counsel for the
respondent/complainant submits that news item would not
be telecast on its own unless there is consent of the
management. The persons who are responsible for running
the programme on the TV would be the Managing Directors
and other Directors. The reporters are responsible for
gathering news item and also news reader for making such
comments. Further, the matter was scrolled on TV and in fact
all the accused had knowledge about the said program, for
which reason, the proceedings cannot be quashed.
law_analysis:
Learned Magistrate on the basis of the complaint has
taken cognizance against the accused. The said order reads
as follows: "Perused the sworn statement and MOs 1 and 2. It is disclosed
that the A2NTV has telecast a news item against complainant
describing him as 'Mafia Don, Kantri, Ketugadu Addagadida,
Durmargudu, KD, Old City don and described him as an Anti
Social Eliment. In the news item it was alleged that the complaint
was manufacturing a Gutka item and branding it as Goa Gutka
and selling the same in the market and that when the owner of
Goa Gutka by name Joshi questioned the complainant, ,he is
alleged to have threatened the said Joshi by using the name of
Dawood Ibrahim. The words and expressions used in the news
bulletin are not warranted to convey the news to the public. The material on record is constituting the prima facie case to
attract an offence under Section 500 IPC. Hence the cognizance of offence U/s.500 IPC is taken by
exercising the power under Section 190(A) Cr.P.C against R1 to
R11. Issue summons against them on payment of costs. Call on
06.2018."
precedent_analysis:
According to the complainant the said news item
spread like wild fire and several persons enquired about the
said news item. His reputation in the society had got down
only on account of such news item being run on NTV-A2.
He also relied upon the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme
Court in the case of K.M.Mathew v. State of Kerala and
another [(1992) 1 Supreme Court Cases 217], wherein it is
held as follows: "10. It is important to state that for a Magistrate to take cognizance
of the offence as against the Chief Editor, there must be positive
averments in the complaint of knowledge of the objectionable
character of the matter. The complaint in the instant case does not
contain any such allegation. In the absence of such allegation, the
Magistrate was justified in directing that the complaint so far as it
relates to the Chief Editor could not be proceeded with. To ask the
Chief Editor to undergo the trial of the case merely on the ground of
the issue of process would be oppressive. No person should be tried
without a prima facie case. The view taken by the High Court is
untenable. The appeal is accordingly allowed. The order of the High
Court is set aside.° 11. In the case of P.Kiran v. State of Andhra Pradesh [2010 SCC OnLine AP 1267], this court held as follows: "4. Thus Mens rea on the part of the accused is essential for
defamation. In order to constitute Mens rea, the accused must
have prior knowledge of commission of the offence. At this stage, it
may be noted that A2 who is the Chief Reporter of Gemini
Television at Visakhapatnam is not the petitioner herein and he is
not seeking quashing of complaint insofar as he is concerned. The
petitioner herein is A1 and he seeks quashing of the complaint
insofar as he is concerned, under Section 482 Cr.P.C. 5. In Para 2 of the complaint it is stated that A1 is Managing
Director of the Gemini Television and Teja News Electronic Media,
Telecasting news throughout the State and also at the National
level and that A2 is the Chief Reporter of Gemini Television at
Visakhapatnam "responsible for gathering news and making news
item from the Visakhapatnam District and causing its telecast
through the Main station at Hyderabad." Thus even in the
complaint, the complainant did not plead and allege that A1, as
Managing Director had any role in gathering news or in making
news items or in causing its telecast through the channel. No role
is attributed to A1 by the complainant in telecasting the alleged defamatory news item. When A1 had no role in affairs in Gemini
Television, no vicarious liability on criminal side can be attributed
to him unless there is any special or specific provision in Section
IPC mulcting him with such vicarious liability. It was held by
this Court in Ravi Prakash v. J.C.Diwakar Reddy, 2010 (1) ALD
(Crl.) 575 (AP), afer surveying case law in the subject including K.M.Mathew v. State of Kerala , AIR 1992 SC 2206, Dasari
Narayana Rao v. R.D.Bhagvanas, 1986 Crl.LJ 888, by this Court, Prabhu Chawlaand v. A.U.Sheriff , 1995 Crl.LJ 1922, of the
Karnataka High Court and S.Nihal Sigh v. Arjan Das , 1983 Crl. LJ
777, of the Delhi High Court."
In the case of Smt. Dipannita Jaiswal v. State of
Assam and another , the Gauati High Court in Criminal
Petition No.33 of 2015 held as follows:
"13. Chairman/Managing Director of a news channel can be held
liable for publication of the offending news item only if it can be
shown that he was somehow concerned with publication of the
defamatory news item and that he had active knowledge thereof. As
held in S Nihal Page No.# 5/7 Singh & Ors. V. Arjan Das ; 1983 Cri.
L.J. 777, an individual cannot be asked to answer the charge of
defamation merely because he happened to be the Chairman of a
company which owns a newspaper, without there being any further
evidence as regards his participation in the actual management and
administration of the affairs of the company.
So, the whole concept of fastening liability hinges on knowledge.
As held in Kalanithi Maran v. A.Rathinaraj ; 2017 SCC Online Mad
9723 and G K Mani v. New General Media Corporation (P.) Ltd;
2019 SCC Online Mad 8332, for fastening liability, what is of
paramount importance is that knowledge has to be attributed to the
accused person. In Kalanithi (supra), the petitioner is the
Chairman-cum- MD of Sun TV Network Ltd. and the complaint was
filed against him for telecasting an interview between the
complainant and one person, on the allegation of falsity of the
statement given in the news and consequently, the MD is equally
responsible for telecasting such defamatory statement. The Hon'ble
High Court held as below:- "Vicarious liability under Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867 ,
is not applicable to electronic media. Therefore, only general rule is
applicable in the present case. To attract the offence of defamation,
the imputation must have been made with the knowledge or intention or at least with reason to believe that it will harm the
person concerned."
The complaint is made on an assumption that the
management of A2, A3 to A5 who were managing the affairs
of A1/M/s.Rachana Television Private Limited and also
NTV/A2, were responsible for the defamatory content. Stating
that on the basis of the program, the complainant's inference
was that the management and the organization was also
responsible and they have to be tried with the aid of Section
120-B of IPC for entering into criminal conspiracy to defame
the complainant cannot be accepted. In the entire complaint,
it is no where mentioned as to the role played by A1, A3 to
A5. Only on the basis of general assumption that these
persons are responsible, they are arrayed as accused.
Admittedly hundreds of employees work to run the 24/7 news channel. Technical persons, reporters, producers,
presenters and several other categories of employees are
involved. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of
Managing Director, Castrol India Limited v. State of
Karnataka (supra), while dealing with a case under Sections
and 74 of Standards of Weights and Measures Act, 1976
held that the Managing Director, though responsible for the
conduct of the company business, cannot be mulcted with
criminal liability unless specifically shown. Similar view was
taken by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of K.M.Mathew 's case. The proceedings against the Chief Editor
were quashed on the ground that there was no allegation
made in the complaint. Unless there is prima facie case,
persons cannot be asked to undergo the rigmarole of a
criminal trial.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Pepsi Foods Limited
Vs. Special Judicial Magistrate (2006) 7 SCC 296 at para-28
held that summoning of accused in a criminal case is a
serious matter. Criminal law cannot be set into motion as a
matter course. In Maksood Saiyed Vs. State of Gujarat (1980) 2 SCR 380=1980 (2) SCC 665 the Hon'ble Supreme Court
held that merely holding an office in a company cannot be
made basis to criminally prosecute holding them vicariously
liable unless they are shown to be individually liable on the
basis of material available.
The program was telecast on A2 channel/NTV. The said
program was anchored by A6/news reporter/presenter. The
other accused i.e., A7 is news editor, A8 to A11 are shown as
news reporters. The reporters would be responsible for
collecting news and news was presented by A6 and for the
said reason of the content of the program being prima facie
defamatory, the proceedings against A2, A6 to A11 cannot be
quashed.
court_reasoning:
Having perused the complaint, the grievance of the
complainant is that he was shown as a criminal and also
several words uttered, which are prima facie defamatory in
nature. According to the complainant, news item was run on
A2 channel and A6 was reporter/presenter of the program
who made such abuses.
conclusion:
At para 17 of the complainant, it is mentioned that all
the accused have telecast the program repeatedly without
proof, making wild allegations resulting in scandalizing and maligning the complaint's character in order to increase their
viewer ratings. In the said circumstances, according to the
complaint, all the accused have entered into criminal
conspiracy for telecasting defamatory and derogatory news
item in order to increase viewer ratings, as such all the
accused are liable to be prosecuted under Section 120-B of
IPC.
Accordingly, Criminal Petition No.11280 of 2022 is
allowed and Criminal Petition Nos.11517 and 11536 are
dismissed. Consequently, miscellaneous petitions, if any,
shall stand disposed.

case_summary: In the case Manoj Rajan Tripathi And Ors. vs State Of U.P., the Allahabad High Court dealt with a petition under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) seeking to quash proceedings related to a defamation complaint (Complaint Case No. 1308 of 2018) against the petitioners for offenses under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The petitioners, journalists from ETV, were accused of broadcasting false news regarding the involvement of the complainant, Sidharth Sanwaria, in illicit activities tied to the release of a criminal, Gurpreet Singh, who was allegedly released by police in exchange for money. The petitioners contended that their reports were made in good faith and were based on credible sources, including prior news articles about the incident, which had prompted a government inquiry.
case_decision: The Allahabad High Court found that the petitioners' broadcasts were protected under the first and second exceptions to Section 499 IPC, which address statements made in good faith concerning public interest and information received from credible sources. The Court emphasized that the inquiry report confirmed that the allegations were based on credible sources and were relevant to the public interest. Given these circumstances, the Court ruled that the proceedings against the petitioners were not maintainable, as no prima facie case of defamation existed. Consequently, the Court quashed the ongoing defamation proceedings against the petitioners.

full_text:
Manoj Rajan Tripathi And Ors. vs State Of U.P. Through Prin. Secy. Home ... on 11 September, 2023

Author: Rajeev Singh

Bench: Rajeev Singh





HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT ALLAHABAD, LUCKNOW BENCH
 
 


Neutral Citation No. - 2023:AHC-LKO:58684  
 
Reserved On:- 06.07.2023       
 
Delivered On:- 11.09.2023     
 
Court No. - 12
 
Case :- APPLICATION U/S 482 No. - 1109 of 2020
 
Applicant :- Manoj Rajan Tripathi And Ors.
 
Opposite Party :- State Of U.P. Through Prin. Secy. Home Lko. And Anr.
 
Counsel for Applicant :- Nadeem Murtaza,Anjani Kumar Mishra,Sheeran M Alvi
 
Counsel for Opposite Party :- G.A.,Ishan Baghel,Mohd. Khalid
 
Hon'ble Rajeev Singh,J.

1. Heard Mohd. Nadeem Murtaza, learned counsel for the applicants, Sri Ishan Baghel, learned counsel for private respondent as well as learned A.G.A. for the State and perused the record.

2. The present application has been filed for quashing the entire proceedings of Complaint Case No.1308 of 2018 (Amitabh Yash vs. Manoj Rajan Tripathi & others) pending in the court of learned Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Court No.32, Lucknow as well as summoning order dated 12.12.2018 passed by learned Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Court No.32, Lucknow U/s 500, 501(b) I.P.C. in Complaint Case No.1308 of 2018.

3. Learned counsel for the applicants submitted that news in question was addressed in good faith of reporting the information to public that the inquiry was ordered by State Government in relation to issue of release of some persons by officials. He further submitted that applicant nos.1, 2, 3 & 4 were working as Senior Editor, Political Reporter, Crime Reporter and a reporter in the news channel ETV, Uttar Pradesh/Uttarakhand respectively.

4. Learned counsel for the applicants further submitted that in the complaint in question the allegation was that on 20.09.2017 at about 2:00 p.m., the news was telecast on ETV, U.P./Uttarakhand projecting that respondent no.2 was involved in earning illicit money from criminals. The same news was repeated at 2:41 p.m. and 6:17 p.m. on the same day, as a result, respondent no.2 lost his reputation and it was also alleged that these news were telecast intentionally.

5. Learned counsel for the applicants further submitted that prior to telecast the news in question, a news was reported in various newspapers that Gurpreet Singh alias Gopi Ghanshyampuria, mastermind of Nabha Jail Break, was arrested by U.P. Police, later on, he was set free by a senior police officer of U.P. Police in lieu of money. The aforesaid news was also covered by renowned newspaper like Tribune as well as Dainik Jagran on 18.09.2017 and reported in several newspapers. Thereafter, State Government ordered an inquiry which was to be conducted by Additional Director General of Police, Law & Order, U.P. to ascertain the veracity of the above incident reported by media. In aforesaid regard, respondent no.2 was also summoned by the Principal Secretary. The news regarding the setting up of the aforesaid inquiry as well as summoning of respondent no.2 was also published by various media Houses including aforesaid ETV. The Inquiry was conducted by A.D.G. Police, (Law & Order), U.P. and inquiry report was submitted on 28.09.2017. During the said inquiry, statements of various witnesses including respondent no.2, namely, Sri Amitabh Yash/Inspector General of Police, (S.T.F.), U.P., Sri Aseem Arun/I.G. A.T.S., U.P., Sri R.K. Chaturvedi/I.G. Information, U.P., Sri K.B. Singh/S.P., Shahjahanpur and Sri Dinesh Tripathi/A.S.P., Shahjahanpur City were recorded.

6. Learned counsel for the applicants drew attention of this Court on the inquiry report and further submitted that as per inquiry report, private respondent admitted that on 19.09.2017, it came into his notice that in Dainik Jagran Newspaper, Punjab as well as Tribune Newspaper, it was reported that Nabha Jail Break accused, namely, Gurpreet Singh alias Gopi Ghanshyampuria was arrested in Shahanjahanpur and he was released by police official after taking money through one Pintu Tiwari. On this information, inquiry was ordered by State Government. In pursuance of aforesaid news items, a press note was also issued by him denying the allegations leveled against him.

7. It has further been submitted that as per the statement of the then I.G., A.T.S., namely, Sri Aseem Arun, it was admitted that on 15.09.2017 at about 12:00 hours, he received information about the possibility of exchange of huge money in lieu of one terrorist. Thereafter, team was deployed in search operation and after tracking the location of mobile phones, it was found that persons were going towards Sitapur. Later on, two persons, namely, Amandeep Singh s/o Raj Pal Singh r/o Bhagbada, Rudrapur Udhamsingh Nagar, Uttarakhand as well as Harjinder Singh s/o Gurudayal Singh r/o 28, Vasundhra Colony, Pilibhit was intercepted at Sitapur toll plaza. The aforesaid two persons informed that persons who came from Punjab went back last night. The information of interception of above two persons was given to Punjab Police and aforesaid persons were brought to A.T.S. Office where they confessed that the conversation was made for release of Gurpreet Singh alias Gopi Ghanshyampuria with Sandeep Tiwari alias Pintu Singh s/o late Surendrenath Tiwari r/o Civil Line, Sultanpur with present address Kumar Enclave Wazirhasan Road, Lucknow. Then, team went along with aforesaid person, namely, Harjinder and brought Sandeep Tiwari at A.T.S. Office. Thereafter, Amandeep Singh, Harjinder Singh and Sandeep Tiwari were taken into custody by a team of Punjab Police at 14:05 hours in Case Crime No.22 of 2017 U/s 364, 382, 386, 387, 212, 216, 216-A, 414, 416, 120-B I.P.C. on the basis of warrant.

8. Submission of learned counsel for the applicants is that as per statement of Sri R.K. Chaturvedi, then I.G. Intelligence, U.P., it was admitted that Sandeep Tiwari alias Pintu s/o Sri S.N. Tiwari r/o Lal Diggi, Sultanpur is his close relative (cousin brother of his wife) who was frequent visitor in his family; he also admitted that he received a call of Sandeep Tiwari on 12.09.2017 at about 9:00 to 9:30 p.m. on his mobile no.9627916006, in the said conversation, he was informed that one person who is relative of Sandeep Tiwari's friend was picked up by police and he was also requested to get the details of such information. But instead of getting the said details, Sri R.K. Chaturvedi scolded Sandeep Tiwari alias Pintu and cautioned him not to involve in such type of matter. After some time, Sri R.K. Chaturvedi himself made a call to Sandeep Tiwari and asked about his location then he was informed that Sandeep Tiwari was in Pilibhit at that time; he again cautioned Sandeep Tiwari not to involve in such issues. Sri R.K. Chaturvedi also admitted that he also made conversation with complainant/private respondent regarding the official work but not on the aforesaid issue.

9. Submission of learned counsel for the applicants is that as per the statement of Amandeep Singh, it has been admitted that on 12.09.2017, his brother-in-law (Sala) Gurpreet who was partner as well as friend of one Rimpal who runs liquor shop, as Rimpal made a call to Amandeep Singh and informed that his cousin Rubal said that his known person was taken into custody either by U.P. Police or Punjab Police, anyhow, he has to get released. It was also accepted by Rimpal that Amandeep had some contacts in U.P. so he could only help him in this matter, at the same time, Amandeep was sitting with Harjinder Singh Kahlo and Sandeep Tiwari alias Pintu in Pilibhit at the house of Harjinder Singh. It was also admitted that after some time, Amandeep received whatsapp call of Rubal and was asked for help in releasing his known person then Pintu alias Sandeep Tiwari gave assurance for giving help and told to arrange some money for release of Gurpreet Singh alias Gopi Ghanshyampuria.

10. Submission of learned counsel for the applicants is that as per the statement of Pintu alias Sandeep Tiwari, it was admitted that on 12.09.2017, when he was sitting at the house of his friend, namely, Harjinder Singh Kahlo along with Amandeep in Pilibhit, he received information from Amandeep that on 10.09.2017 in the morning, Gurpreet Singh alias Gopi Ghanshyampuria was arrested from the bus station of Shajahanpur then he assured that he would make efforts for the release of Gurpreet Singh. Thereafter, Pintu alias Sandeep Tiwari met with Mr. Dinesh Tripahti, Additional Superintendent of Police, Sahajahanpur and after gathering some information he came to Lucknow in the evening of 13.09.2017; he made a call to his brother-in-law (Jija), namely, Sri. R.K. Chaturvedi the then I.G., Intelligence on 12.09.2017 in the night but got scolded by him.

11. Submission of learned counsel for the applicants is that in place of examining all the contents of statements of Amandeep, Pintu alias Sandeep Tiwari (brother-in-law) of the then I.G., Intelligence, namely, Sri R.K. Chaturvedi and Rimpal, the inquiry report was submitted, in which, it was admitted by the witnesses that Harjinder Singh Kahlo, Amandeep, Pintu alias Sandeep Tiwari and Rimpal made efforts for release of Gurpreet Singh alias Gopi Ghanshyampuria. Thereafter, inquiry was concluded with the findings that after arrest of Gurpreet Singh alias Gopi Ghanshyampuria, he will be interrogated for discovery of the truth. It cannot be said that there was no conversation about the release of Gurpreet Singh alias Gopi Ghanshyampuria (accused of Nabha Jail Break case) and the order was also issued by State Government for inquiry. It has further been submitted that trial court without considering the first and second exception clause of Section 499 Cr.P.C. issued summoning order.

12. Learned counsel for the applicants relied on the decisions of Hon'ble Apex Court in the following cases:-

(i) Jawaharlal Darda vs. Manoharrao Ganpatrao Kapsikar, (1998) 4 SCC 112 paragraph no.5,
(ii) Aroon Purie vs. State of N.C.T. of Delhi, 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1491,
(iii) Vijay and another vs. Ravindra Ghisulal Gupta, 2022 SCC OnLine Bom 1315,
(iv) Subramanian Swamy vs. Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221 and
(v) Indian Potash Ltd. vs. Media Contents and Communication Services 2019 SCC Online Del 11991.

13. Submission of learned counsel for the applicants is that in the era of right to information, the person of press or media cannot be put to fear of being sue. It has further been submitted that the benefit of first & second exception clause of Section 499 I.P.C. is to be extended so that benefit of exception can only be awarded at the stage of trial. It has, thus, been submitted that the impugned proceeding is liable to be set aside.

14. Learned counsel for private respondent vehemently opposed the prayer of applicants and submitted that inquiry was conducted, in which, private respondent was found innocent. He further submitted that private respondent had outstanding meritorious service record and he was awarded with several awards, however, the news was telecast with the intention to lower down the image of private respondent that he was involved in earning the illicit money.

15. case_summary: In Mr. Sathish N Vaidya vs Padmabhooshana Dr D Veerendra Heggade, the Karnataka High Court addressed a petition seeking to quash criminal proceedings for defamation against the petitioner, who was the publisher of the newspaper "Karavali Ale." The complaint alleged that defamatory articles were published on November 12 and 15, 2012, suggesting the complainant and management of the Dharmasthala Temple were attempting to obstruct a CBI investigation related to a rape case. The respondent claimed the articles were intentionally misleading and harmful, leading to a tarnished reputation and public unrest. The petitioners contended that the private complaint was not maintainable since it was filed by a General Power of Attorney (GPA) holder, and that the allegations did not meet the criteria for offenses under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) or the Information Technology Act, particularly regarding the lack of sexually explicit material.
case_decision: The High Court ruled in favor of the petitioner, highlighting that the GPA holder cannot file a complaint for defamation on behalf of the aggrieved party, as established in a previous ruling by the same Court. Furthermore, the Court found that the articles did not contain sexually explicit content necessary to constitute an offense under Section 67A of the Information Technology Act. The Court concluded that the continuation of the criminal proceedings would be an abuse of legal process and quashed the ongoing proceedings against the petitioner.

The respondent filed a private complaint under Section 200 of Cr.P.C. for the offence punishable under Sections 500, 501, 502, 505(1) r/w 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Sections 66A and 67A of Information Technology Act, 2000.

2. The summary of the allegations made in the complaint reads thus:

a) It is alleged that the Accused have published false and defamatory articles about the Respondent and Dharmasthala Temple in the newspaper 'Karavali Ale' published on 12.11.2012 and 15.11.2012. It is alleged that the Accused have published that the Complainant/Respondent and the management of the temple are trying to close the Soujanya Rape Case by opposing CBI investigation. The Respondent has alleged that the articles are written in such a manner that the readers are made to believe that the Complainant/Respondent and the management of the Dharmasthala Temple are involved in certain unethical and illegal activities and are misleading the devotees of the temple. It is alleged that the false and defamatory articles published about the Respondent and the temple have not only created fear and tension in the minds of the public but have also incited riots.
b) It is alleged in the complaint that the Accused are involved in the business of publishing false and defamatory articles about reputed persons and holy places in order to increase the sale of the newspaper. It is alleged that the -3- NC: 2023:KHC:27016 CRL.P No. 3429 of 2021 Accused also published provocative sexual images, content, articles etc., in order to attract the youth to read the newspaper, thereby increasing the sales of the newspapers. By making these articles easily available in the internet, young children and a large number of readers have access to read them. It is alleged that the Accused publish sexually explicit and immoral articles which have harmed the wellbeing of society.

3. The learned Magistrate after recording sworn statement took cognizance of the aforesaid offence. Taking exception of the same, accused No.3 is before this Court.

4. The learned counsel for the petitioner would make the following submissions:

a) The private complaint filed for the offence punishable under Section 499, 500 of IPC by the GPA holder is not maintainable and this Court in Crl.P.No.5609/2015 has quashed the proceedings in so far it relates to the said offences as against accused Nos.1 and 3.
b) The allegation made in the private complaint does not satisfy the essential elements so as to constitute the commission of the offence punishable under Section 67A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, since the article does not contain any material containing any sexually explicit act or conduct.
-4-

NC: 2023:KHC:27016 CRL.P No. 3429 of 2021

5. The respondent-complainant though served with notice has not chosen to appear in person or through his counsel.

6. Considered the submission made by the learned counsel for the petitioner and perused the papers.

7. The Co-ordinate Bench of this Court in Crl.P.No.5609/2015 has quashed the proceedings as against accused Nos.1 and 2 in so far it relates to the offence punishable under Sections 499 and 501 of IPC, on the ground that, the GPA holder cannot maintain a compliant for the aforesaid offence.

8. Observations at para 9 of the order made in Crl.P.No.5609/2015 reads thus:

"9. Therefore, the law on the point leaves no manner of doubt that the "person aggrieved" as envisaged in Section 199(1) of Cr.P.C., can maintain the complaint for defamation. The section does not authorize the power of attorney to present the complaint on behalf of the aggrieved person. The stand of the learned counsel for the respondent, that the power of attorney of the complainant is also aggrieved by the impugned publication and therefore he is entitled to maintain the complaint cannot be accepted. It is trite law that power of attorney holder is the agent of the principal/grantor. When the principal authorizes the attorney holder to initiate legal proceedings on his behalf and the attorney holder accordingly initiates legal proceedings, he does so as the agent of the principal and not in his personal capacity. For all purposes, the legal proceedings are initiated by the principal represented by his power of attorney. During the subsistence of the agency, he cannot act against the interest of the principal nor can he ostensibly act as the principal. Therefore, without entering into any further discussion on the issue, the petition deserves to be allowed. Since I have decided to remand the matter, the other contentions urged by the learned counsel for the petitioner are kept open.

9. To constitute an offence punishable under Section 67A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, a -5- NC: 2023:KHC:27016 CRL.P No. 3429 of 2021 person must have published or transmitted material containing sexually explicit act or conduct.

10. Perusal of the article published in the news paper 'Karavali Ale', indicates that the outcome of the research conducted by the Western University has been published. There is no allegation that there is publication of sexually explicit act or conduct in the article so as to constitute the offence punishable under Section 67A of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

11. In the absence of the essential elements to constitute the commission of the offence punishable under Section 67A, the cognizance taken of the aforesaid offences is impermissible. The Hon'be Supreme Court in the case of Shreya Singhal -vs- Union of India reported in AIR 2015 SC 1523, has struck down Section 66-A of I.T. Act as unconstitutional. Hence, the continuation of the criminal proceedings will be an abuse of process of law. Accordingly, I pass the following

i) The criminal petition is allowed.

ii) Impugned proceedings in C.C.No.2984/2013 on the file of the JMFC (III Court), Mangalore, Dakshina Kannada, insofar it relates to accused No.3 is hereby quashed.

case_summary: In the case of Periyakannu @ Theethan vs T. Chandrasekaran, the Madras High Court addressed a petition to quash criminal proceedings for alleged defamation and related offenses against the petitioners, who were involved in publishing objections to a land survey. The respondent, T. Chandrasekaran, alleged that the petitioners published defamatory statements regarding him and the local temple in their newspaper, specifically stating that the respondent was involved in corrupt activities concerning a police investigation into a rape case. The petitioners argued that the proceedings were not maintainable because the essential elements for the offenses under Sections 177, 193, and 499 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) were not satisfied. They further claimed that no written complaint from a public servant had been filed, which is a requirement under Section 195(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) for certain offenses.
case_decision: The Madras High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners, stating that the learned Judicial Magistrate should not have taken cognizance of the offenses under Sections 177 and 193 IPC, as there was no written complaint from a public servant or a complaint from the concerned court. Additionally, the Court found that the allegations did not substantiate a claim for defamation under Section 499 IPC, as there was no indication that the petitioners' actions harmed the respondent's reputation. Consequently, the Court quashed the proceedings in C.C.No.196 of 2018 pending in the Judicial Magistrate Court, Harur, concluding that the continuation of the criminal proceedings would be unjust.

                                                            ORDER

This Criminal Original Petition has been filed seeking to quash the proceedings in C.C.No.196 of 2018 on the file of the Judicial Magistrate Court, Harur, filed for the alleged offences under Sections 177, 193, 499 read with 120-B of IPC.

2.The allegation in the complaint is that there is a dispute between the respondent and the petitioners with regard to land comprised in S.Nos.84/1B, 41/11A, 41/11B in Chinnagoundampatti village; that a civil suit was filed by the complainant in O.S.No.206 of 2013 on the file of the District Munsif Court, Harur, praying for police protection; that the petitioners had sent a letter objecting to the survey proposed to be conducted pursuant to the Civil Court's order; and that in the said objection, certain false statements were made and hence, the alleged offences are made out.

3.The learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that though several offences are shown in the private complaint, the learned Judicial Magistrate, Harur, had taken cognizance for the offences under Sections https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 2/8 Crl.O.P.No.11320 of 2019 177, 193, 499 r/w 120(b) of IPC. The learned counsel further submitted that as per Section 195 (1)(a)(i) Cr.P.C, no Court shall take cognizance for the offence under Section 177 IPC, except on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned. He would further submit that as per Section 195(1)(b)(i) Cr.P.C, no Court shall take cognizance for the offence under Section 193 IPC in the absence of any complaint by the Court concerned. The learned counsel also submitted that the offence under Section 499 IPC is also not made out, as there is no allegation that harm was caused to the reputation of the complainant. Hence, he prayed for quashing of the impugned final report.

4.Mr. Arun Anbumani, learned counsel for the respondent submitted that though the learned Judicial Magistrate has taken cognizance of only these offences, other offences are also made out. Further, the offence of defamation is also made out in the facts and circumstances of the case and hence, he prayed for dismissal of the quash petition.

5.This Court finds that the offences for which the learned Judicial https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 3/8 Crl.O.P.No.11320 of 2019 Magistrate has taken cognizance of, are Sections 177, 193, 499 read with 120 - B IPC.

6.In this regard, it is useful to extract Section 195(1) Cr.P.C, which reads as follows:-

“195. Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public justice and for offences relating to documents given in evidence – (1) No Court shall take cognizance—
(a) (i) of any offence punishable under sections 172 to 188 (both inclusive)of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), or
(ii) of any abetment of, attempt to commit, such offence, or
(iii) of any criminal conspiracy to commit, such offence, except on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned or of some other public servant to whom he is administratively subordinate;
(b) (i) of any offence punishable under any of the https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 4/8 Crl.O.P.No.11320 of 2019 following section of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), namely, sections 193 to 196 (both inclusive), 199, 200, 205 to 211 (both inclusive) and 228, when such offence is alleged to have been committed in, or in relation to, any proceeding in any Court, or
(ii) of any offence described in section 463, or punishable under section 471, section 475 or section 476, of the said Code, when such offence is alleged to have been committed in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in a proceeding in any Court, or
(iii) of any criminal conspiracy to commit, or attempt to commit, or the abetment of, any offence specified in sub-clause (i) or sub-clause (ii), except on the complaint in writing of that Court, or of some other Court to which that Court is subordinate.

7.The above provision (i.e.,) Section 195(1)(a) of Cr.P.C., makes it clear that no Court shall take cognizance of the offence under Section 177 IPC, except on a complaint in writing of the public servant is concerned. https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 5/8 Crl.O.P.No.11320 of 2019 Admittedly, in this case, no such complaint is made by any public servant. Hence, the learned Judicial Magistrate, ought not to have taken cognizance of the offence Section 177 IPC.

8.Similarly, Section 195(1)(b) of Cr.P.C., provides that no Court shall take cognizance of an offence under Section 193 IPC, except on a complaint given by the Court. Admittedly, no complaint has been given by the Court. Hence, the learned Magistrate ought not to have taken cognizance of the said offence as well.

9.In this case, the complaint does not reveal, as to how the objections made by the petitioners for conducting a survey, would amount to harming the reputation of the respondent. There is no allegation to attract the offence under Section 499 IPC.

10.Therefore, this Court is of the view that the impugned complaint is liable to be quashed for the above reasons. Accordingly, the impugned proceedings in C.C.No.196 of 2018 on the file of the Judicial Magistrate Court, Harur, are quashed. This Criminal Original Petition accordingly allowed. Consequently, connected Criminal Miscellaneous Petition is https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 6/8 Crl.O.P.No.11320 of 2019 closed.

case_summary: In Sunil Nair vs K. Armstrong, the petitioners sought to quash an order dismissing their application under Section 91 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) to summon police records pertaining to a gangster profile booklet from 2009. The underlying complaint stemmed from a defamatory article published in The Times of India, which mentioned the respondent's name alongside a list of gangsters, leading the respondent to claim defamation under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The petitioners argued that the booklet was crucial to their defense of truth and to establish their case.
case_decision: The Madras High Court allowed the petition, setting aside the lower court's order. The court directed the summons to be issued to the concerned police officer to produce the gangster profile booklet for the year 2009. The court emphasized the petitioners' right to defend themselves and establish their claims under the First and Eighth Exceptions to Section 499 IPC. Additionally, it ordered that the trial in the defamation case be completed within two months from the receipt of the order.

                                        For Petitioners    : Mr.K.P.Anantha Krishna

                                        For Respondent     : Mr.D.Naresh Babu


                                                          ORDER

This Criminal Original Petition has been filed challenging the order passed by the Court below dismissing the application filed by the petitioner u/s.91 Cr.PC, to summon the Inspector of Police and to produce the gangsters profile booklet for the year 2009, in order to enable the petitioners to adduce evidence on the defense side.

https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 2 of 4

2.Heard Mr.K.P.Anantha Krishna, learned counsel for the petitioners and Mr.D.Naresh Babu, learned counsel for the respondent.

3.The respondent has initiated private complaint against the petitioners for offence u/s.499 IPC punishable u/s.500 IPC. This complaint was given based on an article that was published in the Times of India, Chennai Edition on 27.7.2009. This article referred to a booklet that was prepared by the police which contained the names of 50 gangsters. While making reference to this booklet, the name of the respondent/complainant was also mentioned in the news article. The respondent has therefore taken a stand that this article has seriously affected his reputation and as a result, the private complaint has been filed for the offence of defamation.

4.The respondent had examined nearly four witnesses on his side to establish the commission of the offence. The case was at the stage of defense evidence and the petitioners had filed an application u/s.91 Cr.PC, to summon the concerned police to produce the gangster profile booklet of the year 2009. The petitioners wanted this booklet to be furnished since the same was referred in the news article that was published in the newspaper on 27.7.2009. According to the petitioners, they have to establish their defense of truth and hence were exercising a right that has been given u/s.254 Cr.PC.

5.The Court below had dismissed the application mainly on the ground that the petitioners are trying to drag on the proceedings. The Court below has also https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 3 of 4 come to a conclusion that the very publication of the article should have been made only after getting that booklet.

6.The petitioners have taken defense before the Court below under First Exception and Eighth Exception to Section 499 IPC. The same has to be established by the petitioners and the best way to establish the same is to summon the relevant booklet that has been referred in the article that was published in the newspaper. Hence, this Court is of the considered view that the petitioners have to be given such an opportunity to establish their defense.

7.In the light of the above discussion, the order passed by the Court below in Crl.M.P.No.29514 of 2021, dated 12.7.2022, is hereby set aside. The Court below shall issue summons to the concerned police officer and direct him to produce the gangster profile booklet for the year 2009. The Court below shall complete the proceedings in C.C.No.2794 of 2009, within a period of two months from the date of receipt of copy of the order.

8.In the result, this criminal original petition is allowed with the above directions. Consequently, connected miscellaneous petitions are closed.

case_summary: In Sri. Tukarama vs. Sri. Mohan N Gangolli, the petitioner challenged the proceedings initiated against him under Section 500 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for defamation. The complaint, filed by the respondent, alleged that the petitioners made defamatory remarks published in newspapers and broadcast on Kannada news channels. The petitioners contended that the allegations in their suit against the government and the respondent were made in good faith to protect public interest, invoking the ninth exception of Section 499 IPC, which protects statements made in good faith for the protection of one's own or another's interests.
case_decision: The Karnataka High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners, stating that the respondent had failed to provide any evidence to substantiate the claims of publication of defamatory remarks. The court noted that the allegations made by the petitioners were in the public interest and constituted a good faith defense against defamation claims. Consequently, the court quashed the proceedings in C.C. No. 509/2017, determining that the learned Magistrate's cognizance of the offence was impermissible due to the lack of essential ingredients for a defamation claim under Section 500 IPC. The criminal petition was thus allowed, and the proceedings were dismissed.

A private complaint under Section 200 of Cr.PC is filed by the respondent alleging that, certain defamatory remarks were published against him in the various newspapers and telecasted in Kannada news channels. Taking exception to the same, this petition is filed.

2. Hence, he submits that the allegation made in the plaint, which is alleged to have been published in the newspaper falls under ninth exception of -3- CRL.P No. 429 of 2018 Section 499 of IPC. case_summary: In Satish N Vaidya vs. Mohmmad Hanif U, the petitioner, Satish N Vaidya, the editor and publisher of the Kannada daily "Karavali Ale," sought to quash criminal proceedings against him for alleged defamation under Sections 500, 501, and 502 of the IPC. The petitioner argued that his publication was a factual report of the complaint and that he had no intention to defame, asserting his right to free speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution.
case_decision: The Karnataka High Court quashed the criminal proceedings against Satish N Vaidya, ruling that the publication of the MESCOM complaint did not constitute defamation, as there was no specific intention to harm the respondents' reputation. The court noted that the publication was based on a legitimate report filed with the police, which Vaidya was entitled to disclose. It emphasized that the truth of the allegations could serve as a defense against defamation claims. However, the trial would continue for the other accused involved in the case, as they were not part of the petition.

The petitioner in both these cases has challenged the proceedings initiated in PCR.No.130/2016 (now registered as C.C.No.3642/2016) and PCR.No.131/2016 (now registered as C.C.No.3574/2018) as well as the order dated 24.10.2016 passed therein, by which, the learned JMFC (II Court), Mangaluru (hereinafter referred to as 'trial Court' for short) took cognizance of the offences punishable under Sections 500, 501 and 502 read with Section 34 of IPC.

2. The respondent in both these petitions filed PCR.No.130/2016 and PCR.No.131/2016 against the petitioner and two others alleging that they had defamed their image and reputation by lodging a false complaint and publishing it in a Kannada daily. The respondent claimed to be an advocate, while the respondent in Crl.P.No.5317/2017 claimed to be a Civil Engineer. The petitioner herein was the printer and publisher of a Kannada daily "Karawali Ale" and was arraigned as accused No.3.

3. They contended that a property bearing Sy.No.28/1P6 of Kottekar Village of Mangaluru was owned by -4- CRL.P No. 5412 of 2017 C/W CRL.P No. 5317 of 2017 the wife of the respondent in Crl.P.No.5317/2017 and that various litigations had resulted in respect of the aforesaid property and these litigations were pursued by the advocate/respondent in Crl.P.No.5412/2017. They claimed that the litigations ended in their favor in the year 2015. After a year there from, the persons who were interfering with their possession of the property referred above, joined hands with the accused Nos.1 and 2 to trespass into the property to make a fake show that they had obtained electric connection, just to create records in their favor, which was spurned by the respondents. Angered by the measures taken, the accused Nos.1 and 2 lodged a false complaint before the MESCOM alleging that the respondent and his advocate had committed theft of an electricity meter installed in the property. Based on the information, MESCOM lodged an information of theft before the police and the jurisdictional police registered Cr.No.466/2016 for the offence punishable under section 379 of IPC. The petitioner being a printer and publisher of a local Kannada daily, published the fact of a complaint being lodged against the respondents under the following caption: -5- CRL.P No. 5412 of 2017 C/W CRL.P No. 5317 of 2017

"SÁ¸ÀV eÁUÀPÉÌ £ÀÄVÎ «zÀÄåvï «ÄÃlgï ¨ÉÆÃqïð QvÉÆÛAiÀÄÝ ªÀQÃ®£À «gÀÄzÀÞ ªÉÄ¸ÁÌA Qæ«Ä£À¯ï PÉÃ¸ÀÄ".

4. The respondents therefore filed separate complaints alleging that the accused Nos.1 and 2 in collusion with the accused No.3/petitioner had lodged false complaints, which was published in the newspaper negligently without verifying the truth. The Trial Court took cognizance and recorded the sworn statement of the respondent in both the cases and after considering the oral and documentary evidence, held that an offence under Sections 500, 501 and 502 of IPC were made out against all the accused and therefore, directed a criminal case to be registered and process was issued to the accused. Being aggrieved by the same, the present petition is filed.

5. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the petitioner is only an editor and publisher of a Kannada daily newspaper named 'Karavali Ale'. He submits that the petitioner had genuinely published the filing of a complaint by MESCOM against the respondents in both the cases and therefore, what was published was only an extract of the complaint lodged by MESCOM, which was not defamatory. He submits that publishing of a crime reported does not amount to fundamental -6- CRL.P No. 5412 of 2017 C/W CRL.P No. 5317 of 2017 defaming of any person and that such publication is covered under his right of free speech and expression and therefore, the Trial Court without considering this question had blindly taken cognizance of the offence against the petitioner and issued process.

6. Learned counsel for the respondent on the other hand submitted that the petitioner was bound to enquire with the respondent about the truth of the allegations made in the complaint and he could not have blindly published the same in the newspaper which did defame and impute defamatory allegations to the respondents. Learned counsel further contended that the respondent in Crl.P.No.5412/2017 is an advocate practicing in the Courts and due to the false complaint and publications of such false complaint had resulted in severe loss of reputation to the respondent. He therefore submits that the petitioner is liable to be punished for publishing an unascertained article in the newspaper.

7. I have considered the submissions made by the learned counsel for the petitioner as well as the learned counsel for the respondent.

8. For an offence under Section 499 of IPC to be attracted, a person indulging in slander or libel should do so with "an intent to harm" or "knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm" the reputation of another.

9. It is not in dispute that information in writing was indeed lodged by MESCOM against the respondent in both these petitions, accusing them of committing theft of an electricity meter. It is also not in dispute that this information was lodged before the appropriate Police Station who registered Cr.No.466/2018 for the offence punishable under Section 379 of IPC against the respondent in both these petitions. The petitioner is only a printer and publisher of a newspaper and he indisputedly published the gist of the complaint registered by MESCOM against the respondent in both the cases. There is no specific allegation that the petitioner in publishing the summary of the First Information Report had any intention to harm the reputation of the respondent in both these petitions. On the contrary, the petitioner being the editor of a newspaper was entitled to publish the First Information Report, in exercise of -8- CRL.P No. 5412 of 2017 C/W CRL.P No. 5317 of 2017 his fundamental right under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India. It is also trite that a defence in an action for defamation is the truth of the allegation. In the present case, the petitioner was bound to only disclose the basis of publishing the First Information report, which is not disputed by the respondent in both the petitions. The Trial Court without considering the above, blindly proceeded to take cognizance of the offence punishable under Sections 500, 501 and 502 of IPC.

10. In that view of the matter, both these petitions are allowed. The prosecution of the petitioner in PCR.No.130/2016 (now registered as C.C.No.3642/2016) and PCR.No.131/2016 (now registered as C.C.No.3574/2018) on the file of the JMFC (II Court), Mangaluru and the consequent order dated 24.10.2016 taking cognizance of the offences punishable under Sections 500, 501 and 502 read with Section 34 of IPC is quashed in so far the petitioner is concerned. However, the trial in the case shall continue in so far as the accused Nos.1 and 2 are concerned.

case_summary: In Daljit Singh Grewal vs. Ram Singh And Another, the petitioners challenged the issuance of a private complaint against them under sections 500 (defamation) and 499 (punishment for defamation) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The petitioners claimed that the respondent, an advocate, had been threatening villagers, making false allegations, and abusing his legal position to intimidate them. After the petitioners lodged a complaint against the respondent with the Tamil Nadu Bar Council, the respondent retaliated with a defamation suit.
case_decision: The Madras High Court, presided by Justice P. Dhanabal, quashed the private complaint (C.C.No.56 of 2018) against the petitioners. The court observed that the allegations made by the petitioners were in good faith and could not be considered defamatory under section 499 IPC, which recognizes certain exceptions. The court emphasized that the complaint was an abuse of legal process, aimed at retaliating against the petitioners for exercising their rights. Consequently, the court dismissed the private complaint and allowed the petition, affirming that the petitioners should not face trial for allegations lacking merit.

case_summary: In Prof. Dr. E. Balagurusamy vs. Mr. K. P. Anbalagan, the petitioner sought to quash proceedings in CC No. 207 of 2014 based on a private complaint for defamation under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The complaint was filed by the respondent, who, at the time, was the Higher Education Minister, alleging that the petitioner had made defamatory remarks in an interview published in a magazine, which suggested that the respondent had engaged in corrupt practices related to university appointments. The petition was filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), seeking to challenge the legitimacy of the defamation claims and the subsequent legal proceedings.
case_decision: The Madras High Court, led by Justice G. Jayachandran, examined the merits of the petition to quash the defamation proceedings. The court noted that the second petitioner, T. Kalaiselvan, who served as the Principal Administrative Author, was neither the editor nor the publisher of the magazine and should not be held liable for the alleged defamatory statements. The respondent's counsel acknowledged that Kalaiselvan should not be included in the defamation case. Conversely, regarding the other accused—A1, the editor and publisher, and A4, the interviewer—the court found that the statements made were serious allegations against the respondent and could not be protected under freedom of expression or fair comment. The court ruled that such statements raised significant concerns regarding the respondent's reputation and, thus, allowed the defamation proceedings to continue against the remaining accused while quashing the complaint against Kalaiselvan. The connected miscellaneous petitions were also dismissed, affirming the ongoing legal proceedings.

Abhishek Kapoor vs State Of West Bengal & Anr on 18 January, 2023

Author: Bibek Chaudhuri

Bench: Bibek Chaudhuri

18.01.2023 Sl. No. 06.

D/L. Mithun.

Ct.No.42.

CRR/4680/2022 Abhishek Kapoor Vs. State of West Bengal & Anr.

Mr. Sandipan Ganguly, Sr.Adv.

Mr. Apalak Basu, Adv.

Mr. Zoeb Cutterywala, Adv.

Mrs. Smita Mukherjee, Adv.

...for the petitioner.

The learned Advocate on record on behalf of the petitioner is granted leave to delete the name of the State of West Bengal as opposite party No.1 and renumber opposite party No.2 as the sole opposite party.

The petitioner is the Senior Executive Editor of a news Network.

The complainant, on the other hand, described himself as a reputed singer, lyricist and composer based in Kolkata, West Bengal. He served the Country as a Member of Parliament from Jadavpur Constituency, holding office from 2009 to 2014.

Suffice it to say that the complainant abused a reporter of the said news network of which the petitioner is the Executive Editor. The complainant claims that the reporter recorded such conversation and it was disseminated in the social media. It is the 2 allegation of the complainant that by way of such dissemination, he was defamed in public.

Therefore, the opposite party No.2 filed a Court complaint alleging offence against the Editor of Republic Bangla and one Bittu Roy Choudhury under Sections 499/500/34 of the Indian Penal Code.

The learned Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Alipore took cognizance of the offence and transferred the said case to the learned Judicial Magistrate at Alipore for examination of the complainant and witnesses and further process. The complainant alone was examined. His examination was recorded in the form of recording deposition (Form.M-2) which can only be used for recording evidence of a witness during trial. However, in the order sheet, the learned Magistrate stated that the complainant was examined on solemn affirmation.

It is submitted by Mr. Ganguly, learned Senior Counsel on behalf of the petitioner that the basic ingredient of offence of defamation is that a person should be defamed at the estimation of others. In the said complaint case, the complainant failed to produce any witness to corroborate his allegation that he was defamed in the estimation of others. Secondly, it is urged that as per averment made in the petition of complaint, the accused No.1/petitioner works for gain in Mumbai. However, the learned Magistrate did not take recourse of enquiry under Section 202 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Thirdly, there was no television transmission of such recording and therefore, petitioner cannot be 3 held liable. Fourthly, the learned Magistrate prima facie acted with illegality by assuming territorial jurisdiction on the basis of television transmission of the said conversation though there was no transmission.

The instant revision be admitted.

Petitioner is directed to serve notice upon the private opposite party under registered speed post with acknowledgment due and file affidavit of service within three weeks from the date of this order.

In the meantime, further proceeding in connection with Case No.A.C.1286 of 2022 pending before the learned Judicial Magistrate, 9th Court at Alipore be stayed for a period of six weeks.

Petitioner is at liberty to mention the matter for early hearing after completion of service.

( Bibek Chaudhuri, J. )

case_summary: In the case Shivangi Goel @ Shivangi Bansal vs. State of NCT Delhi, the petitioner sought to overturn a summoning order issued by the Ld. CMM in a defamation complaint against her under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The allegations arose from a familial dispute, wherein the petitioner, the daughter-in-law of the complainant, was accused of defaming him through comments made on social media, suggesting he had attempted rape. The petitioner argued that the complaint was initiated in retaliation for a previous complaint against her and her family, and that there were no grounds for the issuance of the process due to a lack of jurisdiction and failure to follow proper inquiry procedures under Section 202 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
case_decision: The court analyzed the validity of the summoning order and the procedural compliance of the magistrate. It noted that Section 202(1) of the CrPC mandates an inquiry or investigation when the accused resides outside the jurisdiction of the magistrate, and highlighted that the learned CMM did not adequately adhere to this requirement. The court emphasized the necessity of confirming whether the allegations in the complaint warranted criminal proceedings, stating that mere accusations, particularly in a familial context, do not automatically constitute defamation without corroborative evidence. The court ultimately concluded that the impugned order lacked proper legal grounding and thus dismissed the revision petition.

Shivangi Goel @ Shivangi Bansal vs State Of Nct Delhi on 27 September, 2023

                                    1.

      IN THE COURT OF SH. JITENDRA SINGH : ASJ
(ELECTRICITY), NORTH WEST DISTRICT : ROHINI COURTS,
                       DELHI

                                                        Cr. Rev. 333/2023
                                         Shivangi Goel @ Shivangi Bansal
                                                                      Vs.
                                          State of N.C.T. Delhi & another

27.09.2023
                               ORDER

1. Vide this order, I shall dispose of the criminal revision petition under Section 397 of The Code of Criminal Procedure. (hereinafter referred to as 'Code') for setting aside the summoning order dated 13.04.2023 passed by Ld. CMM, North-West, Rohini Courts, Delhi in complaint case No. 8101/2022 titled as Mukesh Bansal Vs. Shivangi Goel @ Shivangi Bansal for summoning the revisionist under Section 500 & 501 Indian Penal Code (hereinafter referred to as 'IPC').

Allegations as mentioned in the complaint for the offence of criminal defamation:-

2. Briefly stated, it is the case of the complainant that the accused has committed criminal defamation by publishing imputation intending to harm the reputation of the complainant. It is alleged that the accused has published defamatory speeches and comments against the complainant on various social media platforms. It is further alleged that the accused is daughter in law of the complainant and due to matrimonial dispute she has registered a false FIR bearing no. 567/2018, PS:

2.
Pilakhuwa, District Hapur, UP, wherein the complainant was discharged by the Hon'ble High Court of Allahabad. It is further alleged that the accused has approached the friends and well wishers of the complainant and stated that the complainant is a character less person and has tried to commit rape against her, which has harmed the reputation of the complainant in the society.
Submissions by Ld. Counsel for the Revisionist:-

3. It is submitted by the Ld. Counsel for the revisionist that u/s. 202 (1) of the Code any Magistrate, on receiving a complaint of an offence, which he is authorized to take cognizance, he shall in a case where the accused is residing at a place beyond the area in which he exercise his jurisdiction shall postpone the issue of process against the accused and either inquire into the case himself or direct an investigation to be made by the police officer or by such other person as he thinks fit. It is further submitted that Ld. CMM has not complied with the mandatory provisions of Section 202(1) of the Code before issuing the process to the revisionist/accused. It is further submitted that the accused is protected under exception iv attached to Section 499 of IPC. Ld. Counsel for the revisionist is relied upon the judgment(s) titled as (a) Dilip Kumar vs. Brajraj Shrivastava, Criminal Appeal no. 561 of 2012,

(b) Surendra Mohan Vikal Vs. Ascharaj Lal Chopra, 1978 SCR (3) 434,

(c) M.C. Verghese vs. T.J. Ponnan & Anr. 1970 AIR 1876, (d) Shalini Mehta alias Shalu vs. Dr. J.L. Mehta (1993) 3 RCR (Cri.) 589, 1993 SCC and (e) M/s. Pepsi Foods Ltd. & Anr. vs. Special Judicial Magistrate & ors. (1998) 5 SCC 749.

3.

Submissions by the Ld. Counsel for the respondent no. 2:-

4. It is submitted by the Ld. Counsel for the respondent no. 2 that the impugned order does not suffer from any illegality as the complaint discloses commission of offence for which she has been summoned. Ld. Counsel for the respondent no. 2 is relied upon the judgment titled as (1) Vijay Dhanuka etc. versus Najima Mamtaj etc. Crl. Appeal Nos. 678-681 of 2014, (Special Leave Petition (Crl.) Nos. 5090-5093 of 2013), (2) Raj Kumar Singh and 2 other Vs. State of UP and another, Application u/s. 482 No. 1183 of 2021, (3) Jagdish Chander @ Gurbachan Singh Vs. Satnam Singh and others, CRR 770-2014, (4) Sonu Gupta Vs. Deepak Gupta & Ors. Criminal Appeal Nos. 285-287 of 2015 (Arising out of SLP (Crl.) Nos. 300-302 of 2013 and (5) Sau. Kamal Shivaji Pokarnekar Vs. The State of Maharashtra & ors. Criminal Appeal No. 255 of 2019 (Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 7513 of 2014). Grounds of revision:-

5. The impugned order has been challenged by the revisionist on two grounds:-

Firstly, that the accused resides at the place outside the jurisdiction of the Ld. MM concerned and therefore, it was mandatory to conduct inquiry u/s. 202 (1) of the Code.
Secondly, that there were no sufficient grounds to proceed against the accused.
The Position in Law:-

6. As per the Section 202 (1) of the Code wherein the accused is residing beyond the area in which the Ld. MM exercise his jurisdiction before issuing the process, the Magistrate has to exercise the following 4. options:-

(1) The Magistrate may inquire the matter himself and if he inquires the matter himself, he may record the statements of the witnesses on oath, or (2) He may direct an investigation to be made by a police officer, or (3) He may direct an investigation to be made by such person other than police officer.

7. The provision of Section 202 (1) of th Code as amended with effect from 23.06.2006, the requirement is that in those cases where the accused is residing at a place beyond the area in which the concerned Magistrate exercises his jurisdiction, it is mandatory on the part of Magistrate to conduct an inquiry or investigation before issuing the process. case_summary: The Petitioner, accused in Criminal Proceeding No. 269C of 2023, sought to quash the criminal proceedings pending before the Judicial Magistrate, 1st Court, Malda, West Bengal. The case was initiated by the Complainant, the Chairman of English Bazar Municipality, alleging defamation and offenses under Sections 182, 211, 499, 500, 503, and 504 of the IPC. The dispute arose after the Petitioner accused the Complainant in petitions and an FIR of demanding bribes in connection with building plans, labeling him a "corrupt chairman." The Petitioner argued that the criminal proceedings were meant to pressure him into withdrawing his complaints and that the alleged offenses were not substantiated.
case_decision: The court found that the Petitioner made imputations intended to harm the Complainant’s reputation, and these statements were not protected under any exceptions to defamation. Determining that there was sufficient prima facie evidence, the court dismissed the Petitioner's plea to quash the proceedings.
